items.title: PAKISTAN’S MIRAGE OF HIGHER EDUCATION
items.description: Twenty-four years ago, on September 11, 2002, Gen Pervez Musharraf signed the Higher Education Commission Ordinance that formally launched Pakistan’s ground-breaking higher education reforms. This legislation dissolved the University Grants Commission and, in its place, created the Higher Education Commission (HEC) with vast regulatory, financial and administrative autonomy, and an express mandate to restructure the national higher education system and set Pakistan on course to become a knowledge economy. Over the next five years, the budget allocation for higher education went up by 5,000 percent. Billions were poured into setting up new universities. A landmark agreement was negotiated with the US to launch what was then considered the world’s largest Fulbright scholarship programme, worth $150 million. Some 5,000 PhD level scholarships were announced for foreign universities, the largest such programme undertaken by a developing country, as well as 3,000 indigenous scholarships. A tenure track system with very competitive salaries was launched to attract and retain the finest academics. To term these plans ‘ambitious’ would be an understatement. Other countries sat up and took notice. Professor C.N.R. Rao, former chairman of India’s Scientific Advisory Council, told former Indian prime minister Manmohan Singh in 2006, “Science is a lucrative profession in Pakistan. It has tripled the salaries of its scientists in the last few years.” This was reported in the Hindustan Times and this particular story carried the by-line: “Pakistan may soon join China in giving India serious competition in science.” Launched in 2002 with unprecedented funding and ambitious reforms, Pakistan’s higher education experiment once attracted international attention. Today, Pakistan has nearly 280 universities, millions of students and a rapidly expanding research output. Yet, beneath the impressive statistics lies a system struggling with mounting debts, poor educational outcomes and questionable scholarship. What has gone wrong? And is there any way out? Bangladesh is a big fan of Pakistan’s higher education reforms to this day. Large-scale academic delegations from Bangladesh have visited Pakistan frequently over the last two years, touring our universities, building institutional ties and doing homework for their own reforms. In 2025, Bangladesh’s Ministry of Education released the draft Higher Education Commission Ordinance, explicitly modelled on our framework. It was an auspicious start, but it was not to last. Within a decade, the HEC’s autonomy was challenged and higher education funding was dramatically slashed. In an earlier piece, we tracked the collapse of Pakistan’s tenure track system and the mass exodus of Pakistan’s best and brightest academics. Now, as our higher education experiment enters its 25th year — its silver jubilee — it is time to ask the big questions: where do we stand today? What have we accomplished? What mistakes have we made? And, most importantly, how do we move ahead? Here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly in the wide-ranging landscape of our higher education system today. LET A THOUSAND UNIVERSITIES BLOOM The most obvious indicator of success is the explosive growth of our universities. As per HEC data, in 2001-2002, we had a total of 58 higher education institutions in the country. This count almost doubled to 116 in 2005-2006 and crossed the 200 mark in 2017-2018. As per the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, we now have 278 universities, an increase of almost 400 percent, an unprecedented achievement. Leading Pakistani institutions now routinely feature in international university rankings. Exact positions tend to fluctuate year by year — and we seem unable to break into the global top-350 universities category — but it is most definitely a win. Student enrolments have similarly skyrocketed, from around 276,000 in 2001-2002 to more than two million in 2023-2024, an increase of more than 600 percent. Moreover, in 2002, student enrolments were split with 63 percent males to 37 percent females. By 2025, this gender gap had almost hit parity, with 52 percent males versus 48 percent females. Another very remarkable milestone is that in our first 54 years of Independence (up to 2002, when our higher education reforms were launched), Pakistan had produced almost 3,000 PhDs. Now we produce more than 3,000 PhDs in a single year. This also reflects in our academic publication count, which has simply exploded. Our global academic publication count ranking has climbed from 51 to 26 in 25 years. As per the SCImago database, Pakistan’s indexed publications increased from approximately 1,600 in 2002 to over 45,000 in 2025. This March, the HEC formally honoured over a thousand Pakistani researchers featured in a list (curated by Stanford University) of the world’s top two percent scientists. These are landmark achievements. Very few countries can claim such incredible progress in so short a period of time. After surveying these highly impressive statistics, one would not be remiss in thinking that our higher education experiment is faring very well indeed. FROM BOOM TO BAILOUT Unfortunately, one has only to scratch the surface to unearth grim realities beneath. Our massive university expansion is now collapsing under its own weight. This issue burst into the spotlight last year with news that almost all public universities in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) were experiencing severe financial distress. A leading academic staff association has demanded a Rs25 billion package to bail out the entire sector. This is not just a KP issue. Deficits are running high in many prestigious universities, salaries are being doled out in instalments, pension payments are being delayed and staff are striking and heading for the courts. This August, the federal government approved a Rs2 billion bailout for Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad. Mounting costs had completely exhausted the university’s pension fund. It was a struggle to fund even basic operations, such as replenishing laboratory chemical supplies. In Sindh, Karachi University reported a Rs1.3 billion deficit, followed by a paralysing strike that made nationwide headlines. The Federal Urdu University of Arts, Sciences and Technology in Karachi has piled up a backlog of Rs1.2 billion in salaries, pensions and other liabilities, and requires another Rs1.7 billion infusion for daily operations. Sindh University’s 2026-27 budget includes Rs3.75 billion in grants from the provincial government and Rs1.716 billion from the federal government and the HEC. This March, the Balochistan government stepped in with Rs857 million payment to 11 universities in the province. Soon after, in a rare and very welcome move, Balochistan Governor Jaffar Khan Mandokhail announced an increase in the public universities’ budget from Rs2.5 billion to Rs8 billion. The University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir has reported a shortfall of more than Rs1.3 billion, with staff threatening campus shutdowns. Punjab University has reported a Rs3.68 billion deficit, which they intend to address through internal borrowing. THE WALKING DEAD — UNIVERSITY EDITION These numbers are just some highlights, but this crisis has been a decade in the making and the entire sector is on life support today. So, what’s the worst case scenario? In 2024, reports emerged that a leading international lending agency — its identity was not revealed — floated a study indicating that around 80 percent of our public universities would default within three to four years. This reads like a mass-extinction event. There are multiple reasons for this. First and foremost, the federal government has capped the recurring budget for universities at Rs65 billion, a limit in place since 2017-18. But back in 2017, we had almost a hundred universities less than we do today. And, of course, in 2017, the US dollar averaged Rs105. Those were the ‘good old’ days. This year, the HEC had internally calculated a requirement of Rs138 billion and had requested the government for at least Rs100 billion, but that requirement was not met. The provinces have also been grossly remiss in their contributions. This trend is not a higher education problem, it applies to the entire education sector as a whole. Last year’s Pakistan Economic Survey revealed that Pakistan’s education spending had dropped precipitously to just 0.8 percent of the country’s GDP, far below Unesco’s recommended benchmark of four to six percent. It gets much worse. To get a sense of this Rs65 billion number, I looked up the balance sheet of the University of New South Wales (UNSW) in Australia, where I did my own postgraduate studies. In 2025, UNSW reported operational expenses amounting to AUD3.28 billion, around Rs630 billion. In short, this one university in Australia — an undeniably good international university, but certainly no global superstar like the Ivy League universities in the US or the Russell Group universities in the UK — has an annual budget almost tenfold what our government allocates to all of Pakistan’s public sector universities put together. THE GREAT ‘SUPERMARKETIFICATION’ Setting up new universities in Pakistan has also taken on an unfortunate ‘franchise’ mentality — as first documented by the historian Dr Yaqoob Bangash — akin to setting up branches of a departmental store chain. Little thought is given to genuine need, excellence and standards or long term sustainability. For instance, last year in KP, with most universities on the brink of collapse, the provincial government moved to set up two new universities. Launching universities has also become a potent grift, a way for politicians and administrators to score political benefits, securing lucrative development contracts, setting up employment avenues and putting the government on the hook. In this model, explicated by former member of the Planning Commission Waqas bin Najib in his Dawn Op-Ed ‘Building the Knowledge Economy’, universities may be conceptualised as “patronage vehicles.” And the HEC acts as “a real estate fund manager.” Our universities are also decades behind international best practices, featuring cumbersome processes and paperwork reminiscent of our colonial era and abysmal governance. A Supreme Court order of 2024 noted that most universities are in contravention of their own laws and are being run on the “personal whims” of those in charge. Almost all public sector universities have too many non-academic staff, significantly in excess of the HEC’s prescribed 1:1.5 ratio of academics versus non-academics. A recent HEC survey found that a staggering 40 percent of key faculty and administrative positions in universities were lying vacant. With numbers like these, one cannot help but wonder: how are things still even working? THE EMPEROR’S NEW DEGREES But, are things really working? A common refrain we academics hear is that universities are not producing skilled and capable graduates. There is little hard data for this claim. Our systems are very good at recording and advertising glittering statistics, such as university counts, student enrolment and publications, but relatively quiet when it comes to graduate outcomes, employment numbers, career progression etc. But, every now and then, we get hints that lay bare the sheer magnitude of this problem. For instance, at a session organised by the American Business Forum (ABF) and the Lahore University of Management Sciences (Lums) this September, Federal Minister for IT and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja revealed the results of a national baseline test of 33,000 final year computer science students from 190 universities. Across 10 employability competencies, only 0.4 percent students scored above 80 percent. A mere four percent scored above 68 percent. Overall, 61 percent students languished below the 50 percent mark. Likewise, the Central Superior Services (CSS) written examination results were announced in August. Of over 16,000 candidates appearing in all papers, only 476 qualified for the next stage, a share of 2.74 percent. This brutal rate is not an anomaly; the CSS exams are certainly very competitive. But examiners noted a definite decline in standards. In a written note to the National Assembly, Senator Ahad Khan Cheema attributed this high failure rate to poor academic background, weak analytical and comprehension skills and subpar written expression. The most alarming story I personally came across is from 2023, when the KP Public Service Commission (PSC) revealed that candidates with postgraduate degrees struggled to solve basic math problems without calculators. In language and literature tests, students’ grammar, syntax and pronunciation were found to be abysmal. “It has been noted that the quality and extent of knowledge of the candidates, having postgraduate qualification, is superficial,” stated their report, noting that candidates were “shaky and lack confidence” during interviews. They then asked the obvious question: “Are the teaching institutions properly equipped with teaching faculty and do they provide a scholarly environment to their students?” These examples are deeply unsettling. And even as there is growing recognition of this collapse in educational outcomes, we have yet to see serious meaningful solutions. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for audits and urgent reforms. The HEC has mandated professional internships and industry-relevant certifications for undergrad degree programmes. The Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, Ahsan Iqbal, has directed the chairman of the HEC to undertake an immediate and comprehensive review of all university degree programmes and curricula across Pakistan to align programmes with industrial trends. THE EMPEROR’S NEW RESEARCH University research output tells an equally disturbing story. Behind the glitzy numbers, the overwhelming trend in Pakistani academia is now to publish papers in journals of middling to low quality — typically predatory or mega-journals — which charge extravagant article processing fees to rush publication without rigorous peer review. The end result is a flood of papers of mediocre and questionable quality, but which nevertheless tick all the boxes needed to get promoted in our system. This practice is not research, it is more akin to a transaction. An entire industry of shady journals now operates, earning billions every year in pumping up the research credentials of academics in developing countries like ours. This practice is widely acknowledged in our circles and is usually met with a shrug. But it has now reached critical proportions that we can now only ignore at our peril. For instance, a study from 2024 analysed around 500 social sciences and humanities articles published by 50 Pakistani professors over a five-year period. They found that almost 70 percent of the sampled papers were published in journals that were unrecognised by the HEC’s online journal recognition system and classed as predatory. Another study, also from 2024, focusing on the physical education and sports sciences domains, found that almost 90 percent of sampled papers appeared in questionable or predatory journals. These are catastrophic numbers. However, these are just snapshots of the overall sector. We urgently need more comprehensive studies to tell us how deep this rot really runs. THE RANKINGS REALITY CHECK The standards of our research output also reflects in international rankings, which specifically prioritise research quality over quantity. The Times Higher Education University Rankings are particularly research-driven and this year they included 56 Pakistani universities. However, the results were abysmal. No Pakistani university features in the global top 500. Quaid-i-Azam University, our highest-ranked institution, shows up in the 551-600 range. The vast majority of Pakistani universities are ranked 801-1,000. The Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) — popularly referred to as the Shanghai rankings — which places a very high premium on quality research, included only four Pakistani universities in its assessment this year: COMSATS University, the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST), Quaid-i-Azam University and the University of the Punjab. All of them were in the 801-900 global range. Likewise, the SCImago Institutions Rankings, a research and innovation-focused system, ranks COMSATS University Islamabad as Pakistan’s best at the 1,715 position globally. NUST is second at 2,126. The majority of Pakistani universities show up after the 5,000 mark. A rally organised by the protesting employees of Karachi University (KU) on July 9, 2026 against the non-payment of dues: it was reported earlier this year that KU is facing a deficit of Rs1.3 billion | White Star THE INTEGRITY DEFICIT Unethical practices also feature prominently in our system. A 2025 study undertaken by the renowned John Ioannidis from Stanford University, a pioneer in the study of research practices, ranks Pakistan as one of the world’s leaders in paper retraction rates (at 28.1 retracted papers per 10,000). This rate lags only slightly behind Saudi Arabia (30.6) and is almost double that of India (15.2). A retraction indicates a research paper that can no longer be trusted and is therefore withdrawn from the record. This could be because of an honest mistake or oversight on the part of the authors or publisher. However, it is, more often than not, due to falsified data, fraud or plagiarism. In their 2025 study, Ioannidis and colleagues matched retraction records against their database of the world’s top-cited scientists in their sub-domains. Of the handful of Pakistani authors on the list, they found that almost 30 percent also had retracted papers on their record. In an article in the renowned journal Scientometrics, Ioannidis again highlights Pakistan prominently in his list of countries where “extreme publishing” is sharply on the rise. He identifies “spurious practices”, such as consortium agreements, self-citation and gift authorships, which researchers use to inflate their publication metrics. What do these terms mean exactly? A recent study on Pakistan’s publication culture titled ‘Research Culture in Pakistan’s Higher Education Institutions’ features a despairing quote by an anonymous academic: “People tend to self-cite or ask their peers and students to cite their work abundantly to appear in the so-called two percent list published by Stanford University. This number game has produced research cartels and people seem to scratch each other’s back.” We certainly have local researchers who are no doubt genuinely prolific, sincere to their calling and their valuable achievements should be celebrated. But our universities lack the institutional checks and, more importantly, the will to stop this unscrupulous numbers game. A METRIC THAT MATTERS When unethical practices become institutionalised and systemic, they invariably get flagged at the international level. For corruption, we have the Transparency International ranking, for democracy, there is the Freedom House score and the Economist’s Democracy Index. For research, we have the recently developed Research Integrity Risk Index. This tool evaluates universities using a metric focused on retracted papers and anomalous citation patterns. Of 19 leading Pakistani universities featured in this system this year, almost all were flagged as red flag (extreme or significant deviation from global norms), high risk, or on the watch list. Only one university (Aga Khan University) was classed as relatively normal. No Pakistani university exhibited low risk, ie “strong adherence to publishing integrity norms.” The results of this index have generated heated debate in countries such as India, Egypt, Malaysia, Indonesia and Morocco. Unfortunately, it’s crickets here in Pakistan. REFORM BEGINS WITH RECKONING So, here we stand today. The bold reforms of 2002 that were to transform Pakistan into a knowledge economy have instead mutated into a gargantuan Frankenstein’s monster, which limps into its 25th year, too big to fail and too difficult to reform. We want a knowledge economy but we do not seem to care about knowledge at all. I have written on national-level issues before — our perennial smog problem, broken elections etc — and I often get emails from readers telling me they enjoyed the piece but wish I had offered ‘solutions’. Unfortunately, there are no magic bullets here. Our problems are immense, fiendishly complex and infuriatingly bound up with our colonial baggage. The only real suggestion I can offer would read as painfully naïve: that stakeholders confront these inconvenient truths, make education a priority — the priority — set aside their egos to engage with critics and sceptics in good faith, and rebuild this system brick-by-brick. The hard truth is that many people saw this collapse coming from miles away and they sounded the alarm, but were largely ignored. As an academic who has worked with government ministries, civil servants and politicians, I also realise this is a very difficult ask. It is much more tempting to set up yet another high-powered committee, call in the international consultants or introduce some new foreign and glamorous system. In short, business as usual. NOTHING NEW UNDER THE SUN It might surprise many to learn that the original architects of our higher education enterprise foresaw this collapse. They even spelt it out explicitly for us in the original Task Force report of 2002, the founding document of our higher education experiment, which resulted in the Higher Education Commission Ordinance and the creation of the HEC. Early in the report, they listed prominent challenges faced by Pakistan’s higher education sector, amid logistical and material issues, infrastructure, governance, politicisation and the like. They noted the curious problem of “[s]trong scepticism about the realisation of reform.” At the very end of their report, they quoted a report penned in 1959 by the Commission on National Education, one of the earliest attempts to reform Pakistan’s education system. And the authors of that particular report did not mince their words, which is why their statements are worth quoting at length: “Education… can meet its responsibilities only if a revision of attitudes on the part of the professional educator is accompanied by a change in the view point of the government and the public… In education, the prevailing attitude of the public and those responsible in government was that it warranted low priority… Although our leaders were now the architects of policy rather than the implementers of the policy of others, education was neither in fact nor theory given the importance that would enable it to meet the needs of a people who controlled their own destiny… “We cannot escape the conclusion that our fundamental need is for a revolution in attitudes, through which the cynicism, lethargy, opportunism, suspicion, dishonesty and indifference that have characterised the outlook of so many of our people and officials in the past will give way to a spirit of individual initiative, personal integrity, pride in accomplishment, trust in one’s fellow men and a ‘private sense of public duty.’ We have no illusion that this reorientation of values can be brought about quickly or completely, or that it can be realised only through fiat, yet come it must if we are to achieve any substantial improvement in our education system or any other sphere of national endeavour.” Nearly 65 years later, these words could not ring more true. One is sorely tempted to frame them and set them up on the desk of every higher education professional in the country, not just teachers and researchers, but especially the administrators, the vice-chancellors and the bureaucrats. It would be apt to close here with another prophecy all too self-evident in Pakistan today. This is a quotation by the novelist and historian H. G. Wells, which opens the World Bank’s landmark ‘Higher Education in Developing Countries: Peril and Promise’ report from 2000: “Human history becomes more and more of a race between education and catastrophe.” This is the second in an investigative series that does a deep dive into the myriad issues faced by Pakistan’s higher education sector The author is an academic based in Islamabad. He is grateful to colleagues for extensive discussions and feedback on this article. He can be reached at taha.ali@gmail.com Published in Dawn, EOS, November 1st, 2026

items.title: FG disburses N75bn to 104 manufacturers, N65.8bn to MSMEs
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Federal Government has fully disbursed the N75 billion Manufacturing Sector Fund to 104 manufacturing businesses, while N65.8 billion has been disbursed to 15,018 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to boost domestic production, expand businesses and create jobs. Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole, disclosed this in an address on “Harnessing Nigeria’s Economic Potential for Greater Prosperity”. Oduwole said the interventions were part of the Federal Government’s efforts to strengthen local industries, improve productive capacity and drive sustainable economic growth. The disbursements were made under the Federal Government’s N200 billion intervention package, managed by the Bank of Industry (BoI), to support businesses, boost domestic production and create jobs. The package comprises the N50 billion Presidential Conditional Grant Scheme for nano businesses, the N75 billion FGN MSME Intervention Fund for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, and the N75 billion FGN Manufacturing Sector Fund for manufacturing businesses. Oduwole noted that the N75 billion Manufacturing Sector Fund had been fully disbursed to 104 manufacturing businesses, while N65.8 billion had been disbursed to 15,018 businesses under the MSME Intervention Fund as of the first quarter of 2026. She, however, stressed that the impact of government funding should be measured by stronger businesses, increased production and improved livelihoods rather than the amount disbursed alone. The minister acknowledged that access to finance remained a major challenge for manufacturers seeking to acquire equipment, purchase raw materials, expand production capacity and create employment. She said Nigeria’s economic transformation required fiscal discipline, monetary stability and policies that supported domestic production and competitiveness. According to her, the government is working to remove barriers to investment, production and trade while creating an enabling environment for businesses to thrive. Highlighting developments in the manufacturing sector, Oduwole said cement manufacturing grew by 11.53 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, while motor vehicle assembly expanded by 5.44 per cent during the period. She added that vehicle assembly grew by 40.6 per cent in 2025, while cassava starch production recorded growth of 474.74 per cent. “Processing locally grown cassava into industrial starch will support manufacturers, while vehicle assembly will create opportunities for engineers, technicians and supply-chain businesses,” she said. The minister also highlighted opportunities under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), noting that intra-African trade had grown by 21 per cent. items.title: 2027: Umrah won’t guarantee Tinubu second term — Phrank Shaibu
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye The Director of Strategic Communication of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, has said President Bola Tinubu’s trip to Saudi Arabia for Umrah will not guarantee his re-election in 2027. Shaibu criticised the President’s religious pilgrimage, saying a second term in office could not be secured through spiritual claims. The spokesperson for ADC presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, stated this during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Monday. Shaibu said visiting the holy land should be a personal affair rather than a national event, accusing Tinubu’s supporters of politicising the pilgrimage. He also questioned the President’s sincerity of faith, arguing that former Kaduna State governor, Nasir El-Rufai, would not remain in custody if Tinubu genuinely practised what he professed. Shaibu further criticised Tinubu for speaking into a microphone in Saudi Arabia while Nigerians were struggling with economic hardship. He dismissed the administration’s claims of economic improvement, saying many Nigerians continued to face difficult living conditions. According to him, Nigerians would remember the President’s prayers in Mecca alongside the high cost of food, goods and services. Asked whether Atiku would have accompanied Tinubu to Saudi Arabia if invited, Shaibu said the former vice-president had sponsored the President’s first trip to Mecca. On Atiku’s chances in the 2027 presidential election across the northern states, the ADC campaign spokesman expressed confidence in the former vice-president’s prospects, saying he was “home and dry” in the region. Tinubu departed Abuja for Makkah on October 29 to perform Umrah, seeking Allah’s guidance and blessings for Nigeria and its people. Speaking to journalists after completing the religious rites, the President described the pilgrimage as a fulfilling spiritual experience and an opportunity to pray for the country. Tinubu said he had asked God for wisdom and resilience to continue leading Nigerians, expressing confidence that his prayers had been answered. “Well, I asked for wisdom and resilience to continue to serve the people. I know that has been granted,” he said. The President recalled performing Umrah before the 2023 election, saying he had returned to thank Allah for granting his earlier prayer. “Prior to the 2023 election, I did the same thing. I asked Allah to bless my Umrah then. He did, and I promised that I would come back to thank him, Almighty Allah,” Tinubu said. “There is no other God but him. He is the giver and the taker. “He owns the power. He said, ‘Use it well. If you don’t use it in accordance with my dictates, I can take it from you and give it to another person,’” he added. Tinubu said he believed God had favoured him by granting him the opportunity to lead Nigeria. “So, I have faith in that and believe extremely well that he has done me a favour to be the President of this great country,” he said. The post 2027: Umrah won’t guarantee Tinubu second term — Phrank Shaibu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: SUNU Assurances, SUNU Health strengthen breast cancer awareness
items.description: SUNU Assurances Nigeria PLC and SUNU Health Nigeria Limited, in collaboration with H2O Wellness Foundation, has sensitised over 60 women including 40 radio presenters, on breast cancer awareness, focusing on early detection and preventive healthcare, urging them to prioritise their health while educating the public. Speaking during the initiative in Lagos, tagged ‘Pink Mic 2026’, Convener of the H2O Wellness campaign and broadcast journalist, Janet Karz Joshua, said the initiative was designed to address the need for women in the media industry to pay greater attention to their health, despite their responsibility to educate and inform the public. Joshua said women journalists regularly use their platforms to promote breast cancer awareness but often neglect their personal health needs in the process. According to her, the initiative was established to ensure that female media practitioners receive the information, medical attention and support needed to make informed decisions about their wellbeing. She said the maiden edition was organised to equip participants with practical knowledge they could take back to their respective media organisations and use to educate wider audiences. Joshua added that the foundation would measure the programme’s impact by encouraging participants to sustain conversations about breast health and preventive healthcare through their radio programmes, news reports and other media platforms. She explained that the campaign would also explore opportunities to engage women across different professions and socioeconomic backgrounds, stressing that healthcare awareness should be accessible to everyone. “Women in the media give information, but are we cared for the way we should be cared for?” she asked, explaining the motivation behind the campaign.” Joshua said. In her remarks, the Head of Corporate Services, SUNU Assurances, Japari Yusuf, said breast cancer awareness must go beyond annual campaigns to become a regular part of conversations among families, workplaces and communities. Yusuf, who spoke on behalf of SUNU Assurances and SUNU Health, said the organisation supported the initiative because of its commitment to preventive healthcare, access to medical services and community wellbeing. Yusuf also recalled losing a colleague to breast cancer in 2018 after the woman underwent chemotherapy and initially appeared to be recovering. Yusuf said SUNU Group’s participation was part of its Pink October campaign, adding that the organisation had previously supported breast cancer screening for 100 women in 2024 and 150 women in 2025. Also speaking, the Founder and Medical Director of HealthRite Company Limited, Dr. Uchenna Anekwuonye, called for greater attention to lifestyle medicine, physical activity and other evidence-based approaches to maintaining good health. Anekwuonye said a cancer diagnosis should not automatically be regarded as a death sentence, stressing that early detection and appropriate medical treatment could improve outcomes. Meanwhile Olufunke Anifowoshe of Matron pearl, said early detection could have been saving many lives and knowing the risk factors such as irregular change in breast size, colour and inversion taking place. items.title: How necessity continues to be the mother of invention in Pakistan
items.description: Nowadays, the sight of solar panels perched on rooftops has become commonplace in Pakistan. According to an analysis published by Renewables First and the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air earlier this year, Pakistan has gone from importing less than one gigawatt (GW) of solar modules in 2018 to more than 51GW by early 2026. It estimated that the boom had already spared the country more than $12 billion in oil and gas imports by February. For a country long held hostage to load-shedding and rising tariffs, rooftop panels are a manifestation of the age-old adage: necessity is the mother of invention. But it appears that the boom has outrun the system built to absorb it. In 2026, the power regulator moved from “net metering” to “net-billing”, under which solar prosumers buy power from the grid at standard retail rates but sell excess solar energy back at a much lower rate. The shift has raised demand for batteries as households and businesses look to store the power they generate instead of selling it back to the government. It also shows how the energy of the sun can be harnessed in ways to address the plethora of issues the people of the country are facing. At the recently held Solar Pakistan Exhibition in Karachi — which brought together solar technology, solar power solutions, renewable energy innovations and sustainable energy products — innovation was in full display. Specifically, it showed how to use solar power to address issues around commuting, cooking and obtaining drinking water. Battery-swapping stations for electric vehicles With the US-Israeli war on Iran and its effects on global oil prices showing no signs of abating, electric vehicles (EVs) have now started trickling onto the roads in Pakistan. According to a recent Dawn report, around 150,000 electric bikes and scooties were sold across the country in 2025. The report, however, noted that despite this, EV sales were still not comparable to motorcycle sales: a CD70 costs Rs168,000, while a proper lithium-powered electric bike costs more than Rs300,000. At the Solar Pakistan Exhibition held on October 10, Bahum Global PVT, a solar service company, introduced its EV bikes with a unique answer to both the cost and the battery degradation problem: battery-swapping stations. One problem EV owners have complained of is the battery “dying” like that of a phone, which makes many wary of being stranded en route. To cater to this issue, Zafar Khan, the general manager of Bahum, told Dawn that the company is in talks with petrol pump brands like Pakistan State Oil (PSO), Shell and Total to install battery-swapping stations. The electric bikes themselves will be manufactured in Pakistan, which will hopefully cut the taxation costs as well. This way, instead of leaving the battery on charge overnight or having to abruptly halt a journey due to the battery running out of charge, an EV owner can stop at a nearby petrol pump with a swapping facility and exchange the drained battery for one that is charged one at a fixed cost. After a successful pilot at the PSO petrol pump in Lahore’s Cantt area, Bahum is set to launch the EVs and battery-swapping stations throughout Pakistan in December 2026. Rocket Choolha It is the story of every household: cooking gas vanishes from the kitchens like a wisp of smoke into the night as soon as the clock strikes nine. Many have resorted to using gas cylinders to cook at their own convenience instead of the government’s. This is where Rocket Choolha comes in: a product by Mesol Solar aiming to provide a safe and eco-friendly way to keep the burners on. Based on the concept of a biomass stove, the choolha utilises wood pellets created in-house by recycling wood waste. All moisture is extracted from the waste before it is turned into lightweight pellets. These pellets serve as the main fuel for the choolha , providing users with a solution costing almost half of what they spend on LPG — which is susceptible to price fluctuations during times of high demand. All one has to do is top up the steel cylinder inside the choolha with wood pellets, add a few drops of kerosene (it can work if you omit oil as well), and light the pellets on fire. The design comes with an attached regulator to control the intensity of the flame; all you need to do is charge the choolha with your phone charger or a battery pack — which could further reduce costs if it is solar powered. The interior is lined with glass fibre, a heat-resistant material also used in protective gear for firefighters, which, according to Mesol Solar, makes the appliance safe to use at home. For now, the Rocket choolha is far from a replacement for the gas line that gives out just as one begins to think of stepping into the kitchen. But it does something clever: it takes what would have been wood waste swept into a corner and turns it into a means for making dinner. Nothing is felled for the fire; the wood has simply been given a second shift. Extracting water through the air With a burgeoning population, Pakistan faces growing pressure on its resources, especially clean drinking water. But what if that could be addressed by something that is available in abundance, like the air? A Nippon Energy product, SkySip is a water-dispenser look-alike entirely powered by solar, making it an end-to-end environmentally friendly product. All it requires is a solar panel and an inverter to convert DC power from the solar panels to AC. The unit then uses clean solar power to draw ambient air, which is cooled to condense moisture into water droplets. The collected water then passes through a series of filters to purify it and make it safe to drink. The range is what keeps SkySip from being a novelty. Although the units haven’t been rolled out in Pakistan yet, the smallest is rated to produce 20 litres a day, enough for a small household or shop. The bigger models climb from 50 litres to 1,000 litres a day, which makes the range suitable for everything from homes and offices to restaurants and industries. Power demand climbs with output, from 250 to 350 watts for the smallest unit to 4.5 to 6 kilowatts for the largest. It won’t replace the pipeline or the tanker. But for clinics, schools and far-flung communities where water is scarce, unsafe or sold at a premium, a machine that turns sunlight and air into a glass of drinking water is a lifeline of a different kind. None of these products are ready to replace what we rely on. However, other than powering households, they show the different ways in which Pakistan can innovate to harness a power it possesses in abundance.

items.title: BUA Foods expands margin as profit rises to N450bn
items.description: A leading Nigerian food manufacturing company, BUA Foods Plc, has recorded an increase in gross profit to N552.90 billion for the nine months ended 30 September 2026, compared with N520.65 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. Gross profit margin expanded significantly to 48.3%, from 36.7% in the prior-year period, reflecting improved cost efficiency and disciplined cost management. The strong margin performance supported an 11% year-on-year increase in profit after tax to N450.47 billion, up from N405.27 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. The Company’s unaudited financial results demonstrate the resilience of its operating model and the impact of disciplined cost management, with profitability improving amid evolving market dynamics and a continued focus on operational efficiency. A key driver of performance was the 34% reduction in cost of sales to N592.94 billion, reflecting lower topline costs and a more stable foreign exchange environment. Further demonstrating improved operating efficiency, total operating expenses decreased by 20% to N66.99 billion, compared with N83.65 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. Selling and distribution expenses declined by 15% to N45.04 billion, while administrative expenses reduced by 28% to N21.95 billion. These improvements supported a 12-percentage-point expansion in operating profit margin, which rose to 43% from 31%. Profit before tax grew by 11% to N480.52 billion, while Earnings per share also increased by 11% to N25.03, compared with N22.52 in the prior-year period. Commenting on the results, Engr. Ayodele Abioye, Managing Director of BUA Foods Plc, said: “Our nine-month 2026 results demonstrate the resilience of BUA Foods’ operating model and the benefits of disciplined cost and margin management. Despite a 19% decline in revenue to N1.15 trillion, driven by softer pricing conditions and subdued consumer demand, we maintained a substantial improvement in profitability through effective cost optimisation, improved productivity and rigorous execution across the business. “The sustained strength of our brands and our continued investment in route-to-market capabilities provide a solid foundation for future growth. ‘‘Looking ahead, we remain focused on driving profitable growth, enhancing market penetration and maintaining operational efficiency. ‘‘While the operating environment remains dynamic, BUA Foods is well-positioned to leverage its scale, strong market positions and execution capabilities to deliver sustainable long-term value.” The post BUA Foods expands margin as profit rises to N450bn appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Reforms laid foundation for Nigeria’s sugar self-sufficiency — NSDC Boss
items.description: The Executive Secretary/CEO of the National Sugar Development Council (NSDC), Mr. Kamar Bakrin, has said the bold, macroeconomic reforms put in place by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu have made local sugar production attractive and cleared the pathway for the country to achieve self-sufficiency. Bakrin was speaking as a panelist at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit (NESG #32), on the topic, “Strengthening Policy Coordination for the Non-alcoholic Drink Sector Competitiveness.” He said the reforms have brought stability to the economy, adding that the next step is to turn stability into growth that works for ordinary Nigerians. He stated further: “Our most pressing priorities are well known: jobs, especially for young people; rural livelihoods; security; pressure on foreign exchange; food security; and the cost of living. “Every Government must make choices among competing priorities. Our contribution as a Council is to make sure that, when those choices are made, the full economic picture of the sugar value chain is on the table. This is because very few sectors touch all of these priorities at once the way sugar does.” Responding to the Summit’s theme of turning stability into growth that works for ordinary Nigerians, he said sugar offers a practical route. Under the Nigeria Sugar Master Plan (NSMP) 2.0, the goal is self-sufficiency in sugar production. Bakrin said reaching it would save about $1 billion in foreign exchange every year and create about 110,000 direct jobs, most of them in rural communities, on estates, in mills and on outgrower farms where smallholders grow cane for the mills. “The gains go beyond the factory gate. Sugar estates bring roads, schools, clinics and electricity generated from bagasse, the fibre left after cane is crushed’’. The post Reforms laid foundation for Nigeria’s sugar self-sufficiency — NSDC Boss appeared first on Vanguard News .

Malgré les démarches entreprises par les avocats de la famille, les autorités maliennes de transition demeurent silencieuses. Mamadou Ismaïla Konaté est avocat et ancien ministre malien de la Justice. items.title: ‘Some members are suffering; GH¢700 a month is unjustifiable’ — NAGRAT president
items.description: The President of the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT), Jacob Anaba, has described the monthly earnings of some public sector workers as unjustifiable, saying members of his association are struggling to make ends meet despite the annual salary adjustments. He said workers earning about GH¢700 a month needed substantially higher increases than the eight per cent adjustment agreed for public sector employees in 2027, arguing that a uniform percentage increase did not address the wide disparities in earnings. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, November 2, Mr Anaba said some workers would remain financially distressed even if their salaries were doubled. “Some of our members are suffering. Those who are taking 700 cedis at the end of the month, it is unjustifiable,” he said. He proposed a salary adjustment system based on a range, with minimum and maximum base pay levels, to ensure that lower-paid workers received increases that reflected their needs. “I will suggest that the percentage shouldn’t be a static one. It should be a range,” he said. Calls for better pay for lowest-paid workers Mr Anaba said the existing approach to annual base pay adjustments did not adequately account for the different income levels across the public sector. He cited workers earning about GH¢700 monthly and contrasted their circumstances with those of employees taking home more than GH¢15,000. “As I speak to you, some people take 700 cedis at the end of the month. If you give them 100%, they don’t even have any money to go home with. So we should have a minimum base pay and a maximum base pay,” he said. He argued that employees earning higher salaries did not need the same percentage increase as those at the bottom of the pay scale. “Some people are taking beyond 15,000 cedis at the end of the month; those people do not need this type of base pay we have given. Somebody is taking 700 cedis; that person needs more than 100% as a base pay,” he said. He said the disparities were too wide and called for a pay system that would improve the earnings of workers at the lower end of the salary scale. “So we have to ensure that all those who are down there also come up a bit so that they can also meet their economic daily activity that they go through,” he said. Questions fairness of salary adjustments The NAGRAT president also questioned whether the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission was adequately addressing the concerns of all categories of public sector workers. He said the experiences of some low-paid employees raised questions about the fairness of the existing remuneration arrangements. “You know, it is called Fair Wages and Salary Commission. They are not fair to some categories of workers,” he said. His comments come after the government and organised labour agreed on an eight per cent increase in base pay for public sector workers in 2027. Mr Anaba’s concerns centre on the impact of applying a uniform percentage adjustment across a workforce with significant differences in earnings. He wants greater consideration given to workers whose monthly income, he says, is insufficient to meet their basic needs.

items.title: Currency outside banks rises 104% in 3 yrs — CBN
items.description: •Demand deposits climb 71% •Analysts highlight cash dependence, financial inclusion challenges By Peter Egwuatu Currency held outside the banking system by Nigerians rose by 103.8 per cent to N4.923 trillion in September 2026 from N2.416 trillion in September 2023, highlighting the persistent demand for physical cash despite the expansion of electronic payment channels in the country. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, Money and Credit Statistics, also showed that currency outside banks increased by 10.3 per cent year-on-year from N4.465 trillion in September 2025 to N4.923 trillion in September 2026. The figures indicate that cash held outside the banking system has more than doubled in three years, reflecting the scale of currency demand within the economy and the challenges facing efforts to deepen the use of formal banking and electronic payment systems. A breakdown of the data showed that currency outside banks increased by 66.2 per cent from N2.416 trillion in September 2023 to N4.016 trillion in September 2024. The figure subsequently rose to N4.465 trillion in September 2025, an increase of 11.2 per cent from the corresponding period in 2024, before climbing further to N4.923 trillion in September 2026. According to analysts, the latest increase indicates that the preference for cash transactions remains significant, notwithstanding the growing adoption of mobile banking, electronic transfers, point-of-sale terminals and other digital payment platforms. Demand deposits rise 71% Meanwhile, demand deposits in the banking system increased by 70.8 per cent to N39.124 trillion in September 2026 from N22.903 trillion in September 2023. The CBN data showed that demand deposits rose to N31.842 trillion in September 2024, representing an increase of 39.0 per cent against the corresponding period in 2023. The figure climbed further to N34.642 trillion in September 2025, an increase of 8.8 per cent year-on-year, before rising to N39.124 trillion in September 2026, representing a 12.9 per cent increase over September 2025. The growth in demand deposits indicates an expansion in funds held in bank accounts that are generally accessible for payments and withdrawals on demand. Reacting to this data, Clifford Egbomeade, Economic and Communications expert, said: “The simultaneous increase in demand deposits and currency outside banks points to the coexistence of formal banking balances and substantial demand for physical cash in Nigeria’s payment system. ‘‘However, the two indicators measure different components of monetary activity. Demand deposits represent bank-account balances, while currency outside banks represents cash held outside the banking system. ‘‘Their growth rates alone do not establish how much of the increase in cash holdings is attributable to economic growth, inflation, informal transactions or changes in payment preferences.” The post Currency outside banks rises 104% in 3 yrs — CBN appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.description: Residents of the Bronx neighbourhood in New York where 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Javits Badu Nkansah Frimpong was shot dead are planning a vigil to honour him and demand action against rising youth violence. The gathering, scheduled for Thursday, November 5, is expected to draw attention to concerns over gun violence, knife-related attacks and other criminal activities involving young people in the community. Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, Victor Emmanuel Smith, clarified that residents of the neighbourhood are organising the event and that it should not be mistaken for a traditional Ghanaian one-week funeral observance. “The neighbourhood in the Bronx is planning a vigil on Thursday. That’s the neighbourhood. That’s not a one-week funeral as we do in Ghana,” he said. He explained that residents had become concerned about violent incidents involving young people and intended to use the gathering to sustain pressure on authorities to address the situation, particularly through stronger measures on gun and knife-related crimes. “It’s a neighbourhood where people feel that there are too many of these violent behaviours by youngsters in that neighbourhood. And they thought it was about time that, you know, they express it, continuously express it to governments to do something about gun laws, knife laws, and some of these criminal behaviour,” he added. Speaking on Channel One TV on Monday, November 2, Mr Smith said the vigil would serve both as a tribute to Javits and an opportunity for the community to make its concerns about youth violence heard. Javits was fatally shot by unidentified assailants at about 9:20 a.m. on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while reportedly on his way to school in the Bronx. Reports have also indicated that he had experienced bullying at school.

items.title: US signals progress in Iran talks to avert flare-up
items.description: US President Donald Trump signaled progress on Tuesday in talks with Iran to avoid a return to war , as Tehran reported “intensive” exchanges while offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions. The fresh diplomatic signals came ahead of US midterm elections on Tuesday, in which Trump’s Republican Party is pushing to retain control of Congress, faced with voter dissatisfaction over the conflict and the soaring fuel prices it has triggered. A deal with Tehran “could happen,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible.” But hours later, Washington’s diplomatic overtures were dashed by a report that the United States had attacked Iran, in what the Wall Street Journal said was the latest in a string of limited strikes it secretly carried out against the Islamic republic in recent weeks. Iranian state media reported five explosions in rapid succession on Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz. The US Central Command did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment. Earlier, oil prices plunged by more than seven per cent on Monday on optimism over a possible end to the eight-month-old conflict. The WSJ report came shortly before polls opened in the midterms, in which Democrats expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on Trump for the first time in two years. Reopen the strait Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that indirect talks with Washington were taking place via mediators. “Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive,” Araghchi told state media. “Qatar and Pakistan are playing a very active mediating role in these negotiations.” Vice President JD Vance said both he and Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more,” Vance told reporters on Monday. China also urged a return to diplomacy , while Iran’s security chief discussed the conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, marking the highest-level move in months. Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said the messages received from Washington were “an acknowledgement of our victory.” A senior Iranian official said that Tehran was ready to open the Hormuz strait, an export conduit for the energy-rich Gulf, within two days — as long as Washington agreed to its list of demands. In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the strait, with demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports. “The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach,” Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters at a briefing. Chinese President Xi Jinping also discussed the war with Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq in Beijing on Monday – the first visit to China by the Gulf nation’s head of state since diplomatic ties were established. “The two sides called for resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, urging the United States and Iran to pursue a peaceful path, achieve a ceasefire (and) prevent war entirely,” an Omani statement said. ‘No compromises’ China held meetings with Iranian and Saudi officials in Beijing on Monday as well. Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security,” Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement. Bagheri told Wang that “Tehran’s stance on defending its national security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity remains unchanged, and that Iran will make no compromises in this regard,” state TV reported. In an interview with Al Jazeer a released on Sunday, Araghchi said Washington must accept a new route agreed between Iran and Oman for transiting the strait. He said Washington must also remove sanctions imposed recently and reduce American troop numbers in the region. Trump has kept up his threats against Tehran, saying on Sunday that the United States may have to give Iran “ the hammer ” at some unspecified time. On Saturday, the US leader said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. Baqaei warned that any act of aggression against Iran “will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response. “

items.title: 8% pay rise: ‘We are not being paid realistic salaries’— PSWU
items.description: The eight per cent increase in base pay for public sector workers in 2027 will not address what the Public Services Workers’ Union (PSWU) describes as the fundamental problem of unrealistic salaries in the public service. The union’s General Secretary, Bernard Adjei, said its priority was to secure pay levels that reflected the needs and circumstances of workers, rather than rely on annual percentage adjustments that failed to tackle the underlying problem. He said the proposed increase would not make salaries realistic, particularly for workers whose existing earnings remained inadequate. “What we are actually fighting for for our members is that we are paid realistic salaries. It is our contention and our position that the public sector worker is not being paid realistic salaries. That is the major point,” he said. Mr Adjei was speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, November 2, during a discussion on the eight per cent base pay increase agreed for public sector workers for 2027. Asked whether the adjustment would address the union’s concerns, he responded: “No, it doesn’t.” His comments reinforce the union’s position that the challenge facing public sector workers goes beyond the size of annual salary increases and requires a broader review of the remuneration system. The union has previously argued that repeated percentage adjustments cannot resolve the persistent problem of low salaries in parts of the public service.

items.title: Midterms : pourquoi les centres de données sont devenus un sujet central de la campagne
items.description: Plus de 40 mesures référendaires portant sur la construction de centres de données dans 10 États seront soumises au vote aujourd’hui, mardi 3 novembre. Les infrastructures de l’IA sont devenues un sujet central de la campagne au niveau local ces derniers mois, et la position des candidats sur le sujet pourrait être déterminante dans plusieurs courses clefs. Selon les données d’AdImpact, 173 millions de dollars ont été dépensés durant la campagne pour des publicités sur les centres de données Data centers fuel $173 million midterm ad war », Axios , 31 octobre 2026.'> 1 . Plus de 80 % de ces dépenses sont liées à des campagnes de candidats démocrates (140 millions), 16 % à des républicains et 3 % à des indépendants. La quasi-totalité de ces supports porte des messages contre la construction de centres de données. La plupart des propositions de campagne visent à interdire, suspendre ou restreindre leur construction. Les centres de données sont notamment concentrés dans l’Ohio, au cœur de la Rust Belt, la région des Grands Lacs qui a été frappée de plein fouet par la désindustrialisation à partir des années 1970-1980. D’autres États de cette région, comme le Michigan, le Wisconsin et la Pennsylvanie, sont décisifs pour l’élection présidentielle et pour le contrôle du Congrès. Dans l’Ohio, l’une des courses les plus disputées de ces midterms oppose le démocrate Sherrod Brown à Jon Husted, le sénateur républicain sortant. Durant la campagne, Brown s’est engagé à « tenir tête aux géants de la tech », et a accusé Husted de soutenir les intérêts du secteur technologique. Dans le Michigan voisin, le candidat démocrate au Sénat Abdul El-Sayed a affirmé, dans un entretien à l’émission 60 Minutes de CBS diffusé dimanche 1er novembre, que la question dont les électeurs lui parlent le plus est désormais l’IA. « Elle se présente sous deux formes. D’une part, il y a les étudiants qui disent : “Je viens de contracter 60 000 dollars de prêts, mais l’emploi que j’étais censé occuper à la fin de mes études n’existe plus ou pourrait ne plus exister dans dix ans”. D’autre part, il y a les habitants des communautés rurales qui disent : “Ils essaient d’installer un centre de données dans mon jardin. Je n’ai déjà pas les moyens de payer mes factures et je m’inquiète de ce que cela va signifier pour notre eau” » 60 Minutes Transcript : Candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers on the Michigan Senate race », CBS News , 1er novembre 2026.'> 2 . Selon une enquête de l’université Quinnipiac réalisée fin septembre, près des trois quarts des Américains (72 %) s’opposeraient à la construction d’un centre de données d’IA dans leur commune, soit un chiffre en hausse de 7 points depuis mars. Ces infrastructures consomment des ressources considérables, notamment en eau et en électricité. La multiplication des centrales électriques fossiles construites pour alimenter ces centres de données pourrait annuler quinze années de baisse des émissions de gaz à effet de serre du secteur électrique américain New US Data Centers Projected to Emit More Carbon Than All of Mexico », Bloomberg , 28 octobre 2026.'> 3 . D’ici 2030, les sources d’énergie non raccordées au réseau construites pour les centres de données aux États-Unis pourraient émettre chaque année plus de 460 millions de tonnes de CO2, soit environ autant que le Mexique. L’article Midterms : pourquoi les centres de données sont devenus un sujet central de la campagne est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: NIA develops mobile app to extend Ghana Card biometric verification to individuals, small businesses
items.description: The National Identification Authority (NIA) is preparing to introduce a mobile application that will allow individuals and small businesses to verify identities through the Ghana Card biometric system without having to access its main verification platform. The application is intended to widen access to identity verification services, particularly for users who may find it difficult to meet the certification and administrative requirements for institutional access to the Authority’s main platform. Its development follows the NIA’s enforcement of the National Identity Register (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2523), which prohibit the photocopying, scanning and visual inspection of Ghana Cards as methods of identity verification. Speaking at a press briefing in Accra on Monday, November 2, 2026, the NIA’s Director of Corporate Affairs, Williams Ampomah Emmanuel Darlas, said the application would provide a straightforward “yes or no” response to confirm whether a person’s biometric identity matches the information presented. He explained that institutions seeking access to the main verification platform must first obtain certification from the Data Protection Commission, a requirement that could pose challenges for individuals and smaller businesses. “Those who will have the certification, we have a platform we get them on-boarded onto. Those who would not have it, we have developed an app, a mobile app for them, where you can get a yes or no,” he said. Mr Darlas said access to the main platform was not necessarily expensive, with charges varying according to the verification needs and operational processes of individual institutions. “The cost for getting on-boarded onto the verification platform, some institutions are paying as low as 10 pesewas for verification services to the National Identification Authority. So it is not much, depending on the workflow of your institution,” he added. He said the mobile application was designed to bridge the access gap and make biometric verification available to a broader range of users. He also assured the public that safeguards had been incorporated to protect personal information and prevent unauthorised disclosure through the application.

items.title: Free SHS food suppliers threaten five-day protest over unpaid 2024 debts
items.description: The Controlled Food Suppliers Association (CFSA) has announced plans to embark on a five-day demonstration at the Ghana Commodity Exchange (GCX) in Accra over outstanding payments for food items supplied under the Free Senior High School (Free SHS) programme in 2024. The planned protest is scheduled for November 16 to 20, 2026, with the association seeking to compel the GCX to settle what it says are debts owed to its members for supplies delivered under the programme. In a formal notice to the management of the Ghana Commodity Exchange, the association said repeated efforts to secure payment had failed to produce the desired outcome, leaving members frustrated over the prolonged delays. The CFSA said it had previously given the GCX a two-week ultimatum on October 7, 2026, to clear the outstanding amounts. However, the deadline expired on October 21 without the matter being resolved. The association said the decision to demonstrate followed what it described as the failure of the Exchange to respond adequately to its demands, despite several follow-ups and the earlier notice. In the notice signed by its Administrative Secretary, Cornelius Korku Logo, the association said its leadership had exhausted efforts to pursue the payments through previous engagements. “The leadership of the Association has at all times acted in utmost good faith in demanding monies legitimately owed to its members. However, the prolonged delay in the payments in spite of the persistent follow-ups, and the apparent decision by GCX to disregard the Association’s two weeks’ notice given on 7th October 2026, which lapsed on 21st October 2026, has compelled the Association to take this rather difficult but reasonably necessary option to demand the settlement of monies owed to its members,” the notice stated. The planned demonstration is intended to increase pressure on the relevant authorities to address the payment dispute and settle the outstanding debts.

items.title: Gov’t targets illegal mining, not the mining industry – Mahama Ayariga
items.description: The Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, clarified that the government’s campaign against galamsey is not meant to abolish mining but to eliminate activities outside the country’s legal framework. He said mining remains an important economic activity in Ghana and has been practised for centuries, adding that it would continue for as long as the country has commercially viable mineral deposits. Mr Ayariga clarified at the National Conference for Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives on Illegal Small-Scale Mining in Kumasi, where he urged local authorities to take a more active role in addressing illegal mining. He stressed that Ghana’s laws do not prohibit mining as an economic activity but criminalise operations that are conducted without the required authorisation or in violation of applicable regulations. “What we’re here today to decode and to find a solution to is: how do we deal with illegal mining? Because we’re not saying that our Constitution prohibits mining. We’re not saying that our laws prohibit mining. What our laws prohibit is illegal mining,” he emphasised. The Minister said the distinction was important in shaping the national response, arguing that efforts should focus on ensuring mining activities comply with the law rather than treating all forms of mining as unlawful. He also said he would personally take a leading role in the anti-galamsey campaign, despite the political risks of confronting those engaged in the practice. Mr Ayariga said he was prepared to move into what he described as the “line of fire” and ensure that Regional Ministers and MMDCEs were equally committed to the exercise. His comments are part of a broader call for local government authorities to work with the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources to tackle illegal mining while supporting lawful mining activities.

items.title: JIT chief issued show cause over delay in submission of final charge sheet in Mir Raza murder case
items.description: KARACHI: A judicial magistrate on Monday issued a show-cause notice to DIG Irfan Baloch, chief of the newly formed joint investigation team (JIT) in the Mir Raza murder case, after police failed to submit the final charge sheet. He has been directed to respond by Nov 10. The Sindh home department had formed the JIT, led by DIG Baloch, on the recommendation of a single-member judicial commission comprising Justice Omar Sial of the Sindh High Court. The team was tasked with investigating the circumstances surrounding Mir Raza’s death and possible negligence in the case. Two previous high-level investigation teams had failed to identify the culprit or establish how Mir Raza’s body came to be found in mysterious circumstances. DSP Lashari is no longer IO in the case after formation of JIT, court told The then investigating officers (IOs) had sought three extensions to submit the final report, saying that they were awaiting forensic reports and a response from Apple company regarding Mir Raza’s mobile phone. Complainant’s counsel Daniyal Muhammad Hussain told Dawn that at Monday’s hearing the complainant’s side informed the court that DSP Sirajuddin Lashari was no longer the IO in the case as a JIT had been formed. He also submitted the official notification regarding the JIT’s formation. He added that no police official or JIT member appeared before the court, although the date had been fixed for submission of the final charge sheet. After a brief hearing, the magistrate asked the JIT head to explain why the charge sheet had not been submitted. DSP Lashari told this reporter that he had handed over the case file to the JIT head so the team could proceed with the investigation, adding that he was no longer the IO. Mir Raza, 25, a businessman, had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS. His body, bearing a gunshot wound, was found in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar a day later. In his interim report, the IO named 63 witnesses but wrote “no one” in the column for the accused. In his conclusion, he stated that despite probing all possible angles, police had yet to find any clue or make a breakthrough. The report also contained detailed information about the case, from the registration of the FIR on the complaint of Mir Raza’s father after he went missing to the handover of the investigation to the JIT. Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

items.title: GPCL reforms operations to boost growth
items.description: The Ghana Publishing Company Limited (GPCL) is restructuring its operations to expand its West African market presence and improve commercial performance. The reforms include establishing a commercial sales department, introducing a digital platform for gazette applications, upgrading infrastructure and extending services to 24 hours. Nana Kwasi Boaitey, GPCL’s Managing Director, announced this at the Government Accountability Series in Accra on Monday. “We are doing everything possible to ensure the company stays solid, viable, and vibrant,” he said. Mr Boaitey said the changes had reduced the processing time for gazette publications from eight weeks to three weeks under the normal service, and from one week to three days under the premium service. He said the Company would soon receive modern security printing equipment to expand its capacity to produce specialised documents. “And with that security press, we should be able to even compete in the areas of the printing of cheque books, and maybe, passports,” he stated. Mr Boaitey said management was committed to transforming the Company into a commercially viable institution. “Hopefully, if we continue on this trajectory, the Company should be able to post significant performances going forward,” he assured.

items.title: GAC raises concern over declining condom use, HIV stigma
items.description: The Ghana AIDS Commission (GAC) says declining condom use among adults engaging in higher-risk sex and persistent discrimination against people living with HIV are threatening Ghana’s efforts to control the epidemic. The Commission said the trends could undermine progress in reducing new infections and efforts to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. “Although the country has recorded progress in reducing new HIV infections, changing sexual behaviour and negative societal attitudes towards people living with HIV could undermine prevention efforts and the gains made over the years,” said Mr Isaiah Doe Kwao, Director of Research, Monitoring and Evaluation at the Commission. He was speaking at the 15th National HIV and AIDS Partnership Forum in Accra. Data from the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey (GDHS), presented by the Commission, showed a steady decline in condom use during the last high-risk sexual encounter among men and women aged 15 to 49. Among men who reported higher-risk sexual activity, condom use fell from 49 per cent in 2003 to 47.4 per cent in 2008, 40.6 per cent in 2014 and 27.4 per cent in 2022. For women, it declined from 29 per cent in 2003 to 26.9 per cent in 2008, 17.8 per cent in 2014 and 10.6 per cent in 2022. Mr Kwao said the figures meant that fewer than three in 10 men and about one in 10 women who engaged in higher-risk sexual activity used condoms during their last such encounter in 2022. The survey also showed an increase in the proportion of sexually active adults reporting higher-risk sexual behaviour over the period. Among men, the proportion rose from 10.2 per cent in 2003 to 11.5 per cent in 2008, 14.2 per cent in 2014 and 15.1 per cent in 2022. For women, it increased from 1.1 per cent in 2003 to 1.0 per cent in 2008, 1.3 per cent in 2014 and 2.2 per cent in 2022. “The combination of increasing reported higher-risk sexual activity and declining condom use presents an important concern for HIV prevention, particularly as the country works towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030,” he said. Mr Kwao said stigma and discrimination also continued to obstruct HIV prevention, testing and treatment. The 2022 GDHS showed that 78 per cent of women and 72 per cent of men who had heard of HIV or AIDS held discriminatory attitudes towards people living with the condition. The survey assessed such attitudes through respondents’ views on whether children living with HIV should attend school with HIV-negative children and whether they would buy fresh vegetables from a shopkeeper known to be living with HIV. It found that 61 per cent of women and 56 per cent of men did not support children living with HIV attending school alongside HIV-negative children. Similarly, 74 per cent of women and 65 per cent of men said they would not buy fresh vegetables from a shopkeeper living with HIV. Mr Kwao said the findings showed that misconceptions and social exclusion remained prevalent in some communities despite years of public education on HIV transmission and prevention.
