items.title: UCC inaugurates centre to tackle food fraud in Africa
items.description: The University of Cape Coast (UCC) has inaugurated the Africa Centre for Food Integrity (AFIC) to address food safety and quality challenges in Ghana and Africa. The centre seeks to research and develop mobile digital technologies enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) to assess the quality of food in real time to strengthen food quality assurance and protect food systems against deliberate contamination and food fraud. Established by the College of Agriculture and Natural Sciences (CANS), the hub will collaborate with key stakeholders, including the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA), the Ghana Standards Authority, farmers and other universities, to protect public health, safeguard livelihoods and strengthen trust in food trade. Food fraud is the deliberate adulteration or misrepresentation of food, often for financial gain, potentially endangering public health. In Ghana, for instance, some food fraud activities include adulterating palm oil with Sudan IV dye, mixing ginger powder with sawdust, combining cola nuts with powdered pepper, and adding flour to groundnut paste while presenting the products as pure or organic. In this regard, the AFIC is already developing AI-powered technologies that would mimic the five human sense organs, namely ear, nose, tongue, eye and skin to authenticate food safety and quality. Reverend Professor Ernest Teye, Agri-Food Integrity expert and Centre Lead, explained that the centre was conceived some nine years ago in response to concerns about endemic food contamination, adulteration and food fraud in parts of Africa. He said the canker was difficult to fight, especially with the cumbersome and time-consuming conventional food-testing methods, prompting the development of more advanced technologies. With the introduction of a mobile-enabled spectroscopic device, for instance, the centre is now able to assess the safety and quality of palm oil within seconds instead of days or weeks. Prof Teye announced that the centre had developed a cocoa passport system to trace cocoa beans to their place of production and was also preparing to introduce Spice Check, a technology to authenticate spices consumed in Ghana. Beyond technology development, he indicated that the centre would also educate consumers about food fraud, particularly the importance of checking food labels and verifying product safety. He said the AFIC’s goal was to ensure that food consumed by the public was safe, authentic and sustainable, thereby protecting public health and supporting sustainable development. “‎All the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) will go nowhere if we cannot have a sustainable food system because food is the foundation of every SDG and so we must look at food first,” he stressed. Prof Rofela Combey, Provost of CANS, assured that AFIC would work with farmers, scientists, industry players, educators, policymakers and regulators to ensure food produced, sold and consumed in Ghana and across Africa was safe. She, therefore, called for collective responsibility in promoting food safety and protecting the quality of food for present and future generations. Prof Chris Elliott, a food safety expert with Queen’s University Belfast, UK, emphasised the need for Africa to urgently address food safety risks, food fraud and trade barriers to unlock its vast agricultural potential and increase its share of global food exports. Despite holding about 60 per cent of the world’s uncultivated arable land, he observed that Africa accounted for less than four per cent of global food exports. According to him, projections suggested that the continent’s food exports could rise to 25 per cent with continued agricultural expansion and modernisation as well as increased investment and improved infrastructure. However, contaminated products, counterfeit and expired foods, poor sanitary conditions, high post-harvest losses, regulatory bottlenecks and slow customs procedures remained major trade barriers. “Food security is no longer simply an agricultural challenge for Africa. It is a strategic imperative that demands sustained investment in science, technology, trusted global partnerships and resilient supply systems to safeguard future prosperity and stability,” the speaker said. Professor Christine Adu-Yeboah, Pro Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cape Coast (UCC), said AFIC would become a continental hub where governments, regulators, industry players and researchers could access knowledge, expertise and technology to protect food integrity. “Food integrity is ultimately about trust; trust that what is labelled is what is contained, and when we have labels whose language we cannot read and understand, then it becomes problematic. “We also need to trust what is sold. We should trust that what is sold is safe. We should trust that farmers and legitimate businesses are not disadvantaged by fraud,” she said. “We must trust that our regulatory systems can protect consumers, and we must trust that science and innovations can help us build food systems, together”, she added. Mr Roey Gilad, Ambassador of the State of Israel to Ghana, Liberia and Sierra Leone, commended UCC for the Centre, highlighting the importance of food integrity. He pledged Israel’s support for the project through capacity-building initiatives by MASHAV, Israel’s Agency for International Development Cooperation, and partnerships with Israeli universities.

items.title: Titres de séjour en France : Me Megherbi dénonce les « stratagèmes » des préfectures
items.description: En France, certaines préfectures usent de plusieurs stratagèmes pour rejeter les demandes de titres de séjour ou pour émettre des Obligations de quitter le territoire français (OQTF). Me Fayçal Megherbi, avocat au Barreau de Paris, lève le voile sur ces pratiques. Il s’agit en premier lieu du silence. « Qu’il s’agisse d’une première demande ou d’un renouvellement de titre de séjour, l’administration fait systématiquement le dos rond, gardant le silence au-delà des délais légaux — généralement fixés à quatre mois, parfois prorogés à six pour les procédures complexes », écrit Me Fayçal Megherbi dans une contribution adressée à Diasporas . Cette posture adoptée par certaines préfectures est « loin d’être un simple retard technique, ce silence répond trop souvent à une stratégie calculée : décourager les usagers les plus vulnérables et saturer des services préfectoraux au bord de l’asphyxie », complète Me Megherbi. L’autre moyen utilisé par certaines préfectures consiste à refuser la délivrance des récépissés de demande de titre de séjour. « En attendant l’instruction effective d’un dossier, les préfectures s’abstiennent fréquemment de délivrer le moindre récépissé de renouvellement. Cette pratique plonge immédiatement le demandeur dans une zone grise et une précarité juridique absolue : perte des droits sociaux, impossibilité de travailler, et peur constante d’une interpellation injustifiée », dénonce l’avocat. Les OQTF, un automatisme disproportionné Selon Me Megherbi, les Obligations de quitter le territoire français (OQTF) sont fréquemment entachées d’une « absence manifeste d’examen réel et d’erreurs d’appréciation quant à leur impact sur la vie privée et familiale ». L’avocat spécialiste du droit des étrangers signale à ce propos que l’application de l’article 8 de la Convention européenne des droits de l’homme (CEDH) par le Conseil d’État et les cours administratives d’appel démontre que l’existence d’une vie privée et familiale intense en France — à l’image d’enfants scolarisés ou de conjoints solidement ancrés — rend l’OQTF illégale, et ce, même en l’absence de visa de long séjour initial. S’agissant des refus de régularisation, Me Megherbi indique que « la préfecture conteste par principe la réalité des justificatifs produits, qu’il s’agisse de bulletins de paie, de promesses d’embauche ou de preuves tangibles d’une intégration réussie au sein de la société française ». Mais fort heureusement, souligne-t-il, le juge exerce un contrôle étroit sur l’usage du pouvoir discrétionnaire de l’administration. Malgré tous ces obstacles administratifs qui empoisonnent la vie de nombreux immigrés, l’avocat a assuré, en substance, que les lois françaises et européennes ont prévu des moyens légaux qui permettent aux victimes de ces pratiques xénophobes d’obtenir leurs droits. L’article Titres de séjour en France : Me Megherbi dénonce les « stratagèmes » des préfectures est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: La policía desaloja la acampada de Sol sin disturbios después de que varias comisiones organizadoras anunciaran su retirada
items.description: La policía ha comenzado a desalojar este martes a partir de las tres menos diez de la madrugada la acampada de Sol . Las tareas continúan en este momento sin disturbios graves, aunque fuentes policiales informan de dos detenidos por desobediencia. Los servicios de limpieza urgente del Ayuntamiento de Madrid están retirando las lonas y las tiendas, escoltados por varias unidades de la Unidad de Intervención Policial (antidisturbios), aunque por el momento no se ha producido ningún episodio violento de gravedad. El sábado, varias comisiones organizadoras de la acampada anunciaron que se retiraban de la plaza. Este martes, la delegación ha emitido un comunicado en el que especifica que el desmontaje ha sido el “último recurso” y alude a incidentes ocurridos en el interior y el entorno del asentamiento. items.title: La bulle et le contrôle
items.description: Testez le Grand Continent . Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois Il y a précisément 60 ans, Jacques Lacan écrivait : « L’omniprésence du discours humain pourra peut-être un jour être embrassée à ciel ouvert d’une omnicommunication de son texte » Écrits , Paris, Éditions du Seuil, 1966, p. 265.'> 4 . Nous y sommes. À travers les technologies dites « d’intelligence artificielle », le texte du grand Autre psychanalytique – que chacun contribue à écrire et dans lequel nagent nos existences – s’objective. Et nos paroles, sous la forme infiniment plastique d’une automatisation de notre commune humanité symbolique, rencontrent une inépuisable interlocutrice. Plus troublant encore, la forme machinique de « l’omniprésence du discours humain » déniche des combinaisons qui restent inaccessibles à nous, pauvres charnels. Récemment, cela a plongé la communauté des mathématiciens dans le plus grand désarroi. C’est certain, ce qui s’opère est un saut qualitatif dans l’histoire du social et de l’esprit ; mais, pour autant, il ne s’agit pas de déclarer la fin de l’histoire. Contre le fantasme sidérant d’une « Super Intelligence » dont l’avènement est annoncé par le président Trump Fact Sheet : President Donald J. Trump Inaugurates The Era of Super Intelligence », whitehouse.gov , 29 septembre 2026.'> 5 et les géants de la tech, il convient de remettre les technologies d’IA dans leur temps et leur contexte. Lacan récusait par anticipation toute eschatologie. « Ce n’est pas à dire qu’il en sera plus accordé », écrivait-il à propos du texte d’un discours saisi d’une omnicommunication. À l’âge des algorithmes, ce désaccord du texte humain est affaire d’économie politique, autrement dit de profits, de travail et d’écologie. Quant à son actualité, il s’agit de celle de la bulle de l’IA qui semble sur le point d’éclater. Au-delà de cet épisode gigantesque de surinvestissement, une volonté de prise de contrôle politique est à l’œuvre. Ses apories doivent être débusquées. Requiem pour un boom En 2026, le boom de l’IA a poursuivi son cours. Les principaux hyperscalers, ces entreprises qui conçoivent et gèrent les infrastructures informatiques et centres de données à vaste échelle, voient leurs investissements monter en flèche. Cette frénésie est en passe de devenir le plus important boom d’investissement dans des infrastructures dans l’histoire des États-Unis 6 . Et si l’on suit les déclarations du PDG de NVIDIA, Jensen Huang, puisque cette technologie transformatrice « aura un impact très positif sur chaque secteur et chaque pays, il ne fait aucun doute que ce mouvement va se poursuivre et [que] nous n’en sommes qu’au début » Bloomberg.com , 16 oct. 2026p.'> 7 . Il y a un point remarquable à souligner : contrairement aux vagues précédentes, comme la bulle Internet de la seconde moitié des années 1990, le boom de l’IA n’entraîne pas les autres secteurs. Elle se développe au contraire au détriment du reste de l’économie . Tandis que les investissements liés à l’IA ont augmenté d’environ 2 points de PIB depuis 2023, les investissements ailleurs se réduisent d’autant. Comme le remarque David Rosenberg, fondateur et stratège en chef de Rosenberg Research “Cracks Are Emerging, You Just Need to Be Paying Attention” », The Market , 30 septembre 2026.'> 8 , « au cours de l’année écoulée, la croissance économique [des États-Unis] n’a eu que deux moteurs. L’un d’eux est le boom des dépenses en capital et de la construction de centres de données en IA. L’autre est l’entraînement de la hausse de la valeur des actions sur les dépenses des plus riches, un effet de richesse qui est lui-même alimenté par le boom de l’IA. En somme, les États-Unis sont devenus une économie tirée par un seul secteur ». À travers ce nouveau boom, on assiste ainsi à un pivot du mode de développement, qui positionne cette technologie générique au centre de l’accumulation du capital. Destinée à informer toutes les dimensions de l’activité sociale, ses potentialités sont également si extraordinaires que celle-ci appelle à coloniser l’orbite de notre planète pour y puiser l’électricité que la Terre ne suffit pas à lui offrir The case for data centers in space », McKinsey & Company , 8 mai 2026.'> 9 . Des fissures sur le front financier Google, Amazon et SpaceX ont la tête dans les étoiles. Car, il faut bien le dire, ce boom défie jusqu’ici les lois de la gravité financière. Chaque mois, c’est plus d'argent investi dans l’écosystème IA, mais aussi plus d’argent sortant, sous forme de profits de papier – empochés par des investisseurs, qui ont la sagesse de retirer à temps des plus-values mirifiques. Dans le langage prudent des analystes de la Banque des règlements internationaux, il s’agit d’un « investissement excessif » BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 », BIS , 28 juin 2026.'> 10 . Le procédé employé donne déjà la fin de l’histoire : « La concurrence qui nourrit les excès du boom, est aussi celle qui nourrit les fragilités financières qui vont faire éclater la bulle ». Devenues durant l’automne des fissures ouvertes, ces fragilités sont de trois ordres. Une première tient à la circularité des rapports financiers et commerciaux Joining the dots between big AI », Financial Times , 18 septembre 2026.'> 11 entre les concepteurs de puces (NVIDIA, AMD…), les développeurs de modèles d’IA (OpenAI, Anthropic…) et les opérateurs de centres de données. Pour ces derniers, il peut s'agir tout aussi bien des Big Tech (Amazon, Google, Microsoft) que d’entreprises pour lesquelles la location des capacités des centres de données constitue l’activité essentielle (Oracle, le néo-cloud Coreweave, etc.). Les montants engagés sont considérables. Donnons quelques chiffres, pour saisir leur ordre de grandeur. Depuis 2025, NVDIA a annoncé des investissements à hauteur de 130 milliards de dollars dans OpenAI. OpenAI a pour sa part précommandé 250 milliards de capacités de calcul et de services cloud auprès de Microsoft ; la firme a également annoncé un accord d’un montant de 300 milliards sur cinq ans avec Oracle. Et, de leur côté, Oracle et Microsoft sont des clients essentiels de NVIDIA – Microsoft représente à lui seul 22 % du revenu du leader. En principe, il n’y a rien de surprenant à ce que les complémentarités conduisent ces entreprises à établir de forts liens capitalistiques et contractuels. Les montants et la concentration sont cependant très inhabituels. Si un acteur se trouve en difficulté, c’est ainsi l’ensemble de l’écosystème qui risque d’être déstabilisé. La deuxième fragilité tient à la dette elle-même. Les deals circulaires servent de garantie pour lever des fonds sur les marchés financiers. Et là encore, les montants sont considérables. Le fonds KKR estime que l’encours de la dette liée à l’IA aux États-Unis s’établit à 600 milliards de dollars en septembre 2026 KKR warns of growing credit market risks from AI borrowing spree », Financial Times , 30 septembre 2026.'> 12 . C’est moins que l’encours de crédit immobilier subprime aux États-Unis, qui était de 800 milliards – soit 1300 milliards en valeur corrigée de l’inflation BIS Quarterly Review December , 2018, p. 46.'> 13 . Cette dette ne couvre cependant qu’une petite part de l’exposition effective du secteur à un retournement de dynamique. Pour les hyperscalers, la somme des engagements hors bilan – tels que des garanties de crédit et des promesses d’achat, ainsi que des contrats de location – dépasse les 3 000 milliards Big Tech uses guarantees to keep $300bn of AI exposure off balance sheets », Financial Times , 20 septembre 2026.'> 14 . Autrement dit, il s’agit de montants qui nous amènent très au-delà du poids du segment des subprimes en 2007. Comme à la veille de 2007, les montages deviennent de plus en plus audacieux à mesure que la bulle gonfle. L’architecture d’un récent deal de plus de 150 milliards de dollars Inside Google’s $200bn Wall Street finance machine for Anthropic », Financial Times , 2 novembre 2026.'> 15 liant Google, Broadcom et Anthropic en témoigne : Google et Broadcom fournissent les puces, officiellement possédées par un Special-Purpose Vehicle (SPV), une société ad hoc ; et Anthropic s’engage ensuite à louer ces puces. Le détour par un SPV permet ainsi de lever de la dette hors du bilan des trois entreprises. Dans cet arrangement imaginé par la banque Morgan Stanley, ce sont les vendeurs eux-mêmes qui sont à l’origine du système leur permettant de financer l’écoulement de leur marchandise. Et ceux qui apportent les financements sont les fonds d’investissement Apollo et Blackstone qui, pour acheter les puces et les capacités des centres de données, puisent dans les grands pools d’épargne – tels que des assureurs, des fonds de pension et souverains. Ils contractent de surcroît des crédits auprès de grandes banques pour faire jouer un effet de levier, et ainsi gonfler les rendements. L’astuce de toute cette ingénierie financière consiste à transformer les revenus erratiques des fournisseurs de modèles IA comme Anthropic, en loyers dont la régularité et la prévisibilité sied aux fonds spécialisés sur les infrastructures Our Lives in Their Portfolios : Why Asset Managers Own the World , s.l., Verso Books, 2023.'> 16 . L’enjeu est aussi de contenir le coût de financement, en attirant suffisamment de capital. Les grandes firmes vendeuses, comme Broadcom ou NVIDIA NVIDIA AI Factory Compute Is Becoming an Investable Asset Class », NVIDIA Blog , 11 août 2026.'> 17 , fournissent ainsi des garanties partielles sur cette dette. Les puces elles-mêmes sont quant à ces dernières, proposées comme des garanties collatérales sur les prêts The AI industry’s gigantic debts are making investors nervous », The Economist , 18 octobre 2026.'> 18 . Une technique complémentaire, déjà expérimentée lors des subprimes, est à nouveau mobilisée. On retrouve tout d’abord le schéma de sécuritisation classique, où consortiums bancaires ou fonds de finance privés fabriquent la dette avant de la distribuer à des investisseurs institutionnels Banks lend $18 billion for Oracle-tied data center project, Bloomberg News reports », Reuters , 7 novembre 2025.'> 19 . Ensuite, comme à la fameuse époque des produits « sac de merde », « holocauste nucléaire » ou « coup de poing de Tyso » Financial Crisis Lawsuit Suggests Bad Behavior at Morgan Stanley », DealBook, The New York Times , 23 janvier 2013.'> 20 , la dette liée à l’IA est fréquemment empaquetée dans des produits structurés tels que des Collateralized Loan Obligations , sans que ceux qui achètent ces cocktails de titres composites ne connaissent leur exposition effective Bloomberg.com , 29 sept. 2026.'> 21 . Bref, comme à l’époque des subprimes, la machine financière tente de distribuer le risque pour prolonger le boom. Aujourd’hui, la contamination est devenue globale. Comme le résume Robert Armstrong Who’s paying for the AI build-out ? Probably you », Financial Times , 21 octobre 2026.'> 22 , « Chaque grand pool de capitaux, aux quatre coins du monde développé, finance des centres de données ». C’est ainsi qu’apparaît la troisième fissure : ce prolongement devient en effet de plus en plus précaire du fait de l’augmentation des taux d’intérêt. Dans un contexte global de renchérissement de la dette, les taux exigés pour le système d’IA progressent davantage, et le coût de l’assurance contre le risque de défaut de paiement (les Credit Default Swaps, CDS) encore plus. Pour les hyperscalers, la hausse de la prime de risque est notable The Limits of AI Debt as a Driver of Treasury Yields », MSCI , 3 septembre 2026.'> 23 ; et surtout, l’augmentation du volume et du coût de l’assurance contre un défaut AI debt worries spark surge in default insurance trading », Financial Times , 19 octobre 2026.'> 24 a considérablement cru ces derniers mois, jusqu’à atteindre environ 1 % pour Meta et NVIDIA, soit une probabilité de défaut à cinq ans de l’ordre de 8 %. Pour les acteurs les plus exposés comme le neocloud Coreweave, l’évolution est brutale CoreWeave Credit Risk Hits Record as Default Odds Top 60 % on Borrowing Plans », Bloomberg , 15 octobre 2026.'> 25 : mi-octobre, le rendement exigé pour certains titres à 5 ans était de 14,5 %, tandis que l’envolée des CDS équivaut à une probabilité de défaut sur la même période de 60 %. À un tel niveau, l’étranglement financier est presque garanti. Complications opérationnelles Tout comme au printemps 2007, les signaux de fragilité clignotent avec de plus en plus d’insistance. Ils signalent des contradictions bien réelles entre les attentes nourries par les investisseurs et les conditions concrètes de valorisation. Sur le moyen terme, l’empreinte écologique de l’IA en termes d’émission de gaz à effet de serre, d’utilisation d’eau, mais aussi d’extraction de minerais et de déchets électroniques Resources, Conservation and Recycling , 1 avril 2026, vol. 229, p. 108872.'> 26 , trace une trajectoire insoutenable. Mais dans l’immédiat, les facteurs de crise tiennent à l’impossibilité de déployer une puissance de calcul à la hauteur des financements levés et aux incertitudes sur la possibilité de dégager des profits conformes aux profits escomptés. Le problème le plus flagrant réside dans le décalage entre les dépenses d’investissement et les capacités effectivement construites. Aux États-Unis, mais pas seulement AI Data Center Backlash Threatens Australia’s $70 Billion Dream », Bloomberg , 22 octobre 2026.'> 27 , les retards de chantiers se multiplient. On observe une déconnexion croissante entre les dépenses engagées et les capacités effectivement ajoutées. À quoi correspondent ces dépenses d’« investissements en construction » ? Pour l’essentiel, il s’agit d’un stockage massif de puces destinées à l’IA. Loin d’être marginal, ce phénomène de « dark GPUs » Amazon is buying billions in Nvidia AI systems it can’t yet turn on », Business Insider , 20 octobre 2026.'> 28 – c’est-à-dire, de puces acquises, mais non utilisées – est évalué à 234 milliards de dollars Where’re All The AI Chips ? », Where’s Your Ed At , 22 septembre 2026'> 29 , soit 50 % de la valeur totale des puces vendues par NVIDIA et Broadcom depuis début 2023. De tels niveaux de stockage suggèrent clairement que la spéculation a pris le pas. En effet, pourquoi acquérir des puces qu’on ne peut utiliser, si ce n’est dans l’espoir de les revendre plus cher ou de les déployer dans des conditions plus favorables ? On peut s’interroger sur ce qui garantit que ces conditions favorables se réaliseront dans un horizon compatible avec les espérances de profits. De multiples raisons expliquent pourquoi la construction des centres de données prend du retard. Certaines sont purement opérationnelles. Cela peut être en raison d’un nombre insuffisant de travailleurs qualifiés, de réseaux électriques sous tension, ou encore, de pénuries d’équipements tels que les turbines à gaz et les transformateurs électriques. Mais l’obstacle le plus important – et identifié comme tel par Anthropic dans les documents préparatoires à son entrée en bourse Anthropic S-1 Shows Red-Hot Growth, Risks and Massive Computing Costs », The Wall Street Journal , 20 octobre 2026. '> 30 –, découle de l’hostilité croissante des populations . Ces infrastructures sont connues en effet pour renchérir le coût de l’électricité, pour prélever de précieuses ressources en eau et pour empiéter sur le foncier. Afin de contrer leur construction, la résistance populaire prend ainsi de l’ampleur The Accidental Activists of Data Center Alley », The Nation , 21 octobre 2026.'> 31 . Les recours juridiques se multiplient, et la pression conduit les administrations à annoncer des mesures restrictives. Ainsi, des moratoires sont désormais en vigueur dans 22 États – dont la Californie, l'État de New York ou encore le Texas Data Center Moratoriums », datacenterbans.com , consulté le 2 novembre 2026.'> 32 . La rentabilité en question Les secondes incertitudes portent sur la solidité des projections de revenus ; des béances apparaissent tant du côté de la demande que de l’offre. Les anticipations qui sous-tendent les investissements colossaux engagés, impliquent plusieurs choses. D’abord, les avantages qui découlent de l’utilisation des services d’IA, doivent être suffisamment importants pour soutenir une demande dynamique et durable. De nombreuses études de cas et de récits circonstanciels témoignent de progrès épatants dans l’efficacité du travail. On le remarque par exemple chez les opérateurs des plateformes téléphoniques The Quarterly Journal of Economics , 2025.'> 33 , chez les ingénieurs informatiques Management Science , 27 février 2026.'> 34 , ou de manière plus anecdotique, dans la communication d’une artisane-graveuse sur bois et acier Rencontres régionales de l’Economie : l’artisanat face au défi de l’Intelligence Artificielle (IA) », Coup de main , CMA Hauts-de-France, 28 février 2025.'> 35 , par exemple. Cependant, passer du niveau d’une tâche précise à celui des grandes organisations – et a fortiori de l’économie dans son ensemble –, ne va pas de soi. Si les économistes anticipent des progrès modérés arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.14588 , 2025 ; Kristina McElheran et al., The Rise of Industrial AI in America : Microfoundations of the Productivity J-curve (s) , s.l., US Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies, 2025.'> 36 , les études empiriques sont ambivalentes FEDS Notes. , 17 juillet 2026.'> 37 . Et pour l’instant, les gains ne se concrétisent pas à grande échelle Have We Entered an Era of High Productivity Growth ? », FRBSF Economic Letter , 2026-14, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, 26 mai 2026.'> 38 . Quarante ans après sa première énoncé, on peut ainsi paraphraser le célèbre paradoxe de Solow : l’IA est partout, sauf dans les statistiques de productivité. Comme le résume l’économiste en chef d’un gestionnaire d’actifs Slowing Token Spend Shows Compute Demand Isn’t Unlimited », The Daily Spark ,Apollo,20 octobre 2026.'> 39 , « l’erreur économique fondamentale de l’argument optimiste concernant l'IA, tient au fait que le coût marginal de la production du calcul dépasse le bénéfice marginal apporté aux utilisateurs ». Autrement dit, cela coûte plus cher à produire que cela ne rapporte aux clients. Si tel est le cas, l’idée que la demande pour les puces et les centres de données serait illimitée est fausse. La question qui se pose alors, est d’une simplicité déroutante : est-ce rentable ? Les incertitudes en termes de coût et d’usage se traduisent au niveau du système de prix dans l’absence de stabilisation des méthodes de tarification. À l’inverse, à Washington, le développement du secteur est exclusivement conçu à l’aune de la rivalité stratégique avec la Chine. À ce titre, l’État fédéral garantit un soutien sans limite aux firmes du secteur via la Mission Genesis du département de l’Énergie Launching the Genesis Mission , 24 novembre 2025'> 88 . À l’échelle internationale, l’administration opère une manœuvre de containment via la création d’un espace technologique et sécuritaire nommé Pax Silica Pax Silica , 2026.'> 89 . On peut craindre que ce cadre n’emprisonne les pays qui y consentent dans les enclosures intellectuelles de l’écosystème numérique étatsunien et ne contribue à fracturer durablement deux pôles géopolitiques antagoniques. Enfin, sur un troisième et dernier plan, celui des modes de déploiement de la technologie, la Chine semble aussi se démarquer de la voie étatsunienne. Alors qu’outre-Atlantique, on l’a vu, l’accent est mis sur la possibilité de la superintelligence et de la singularité, l’approche chinoise se veut plus pragmatique et centrée sur l’automatisation des différents processus industriels. C’est le sens de l’initiative IA Plus China’s “AI+” drive aims for integration across sectors : a wake-up call for Europe », MERICS , 2 octobre 2025.'> 90 qui définit des objectifs et des standards de déploiement de l’IA par secteur, une approche sans doute plus à même d’aligner investissements et perspectives de valorisation. C’est aussi une des raisons pour lesquelles le montant brut des dépenses d’investissement en matière d’IA en Chine reste loin de celui engagé aux États-Unis Punching above their weight : how China’s AI giants stretch each dollar in computerace », South China Morning Post , 6 septembre 2026.'> 91 , quand bien même le pays se rapproche de la frontière technologique. Une grande crise À l’issue de ce panorama concernant l’évolution récente de l’économie politique de l’IA, nous pouvons tirer quelques conclusions. La première consiste simplement à rappeler que le destin de l’humanité est d’abord entre les mains des humains et qu’il n’y a pas de fatalisme technologique . Au-delà des prouesses de l’IA, les tensions qui découlent des masses financières requises, des ressources matérielles prélevées et des mutations des relations sociales, constituent autant de facteurs générateurs d’une crise. Ses prémices se manifestent déjà et vont appeler des réorganisations d’ampleur. Compte tenu des montants en jeu, il est difficile de ne pas établir une comparaison avec la déflagration de 2007-2008, même si l’épicentre s’est déplacé de l’immobilier à la tech et que les conditions à la fois géopolitiques, macroéconomiques et monétaires diffèrent substantiellement. À l’époque, le choix a été fait de sauver le système financier en soutenant les banques, plutôt que les emprunteurs. Aujourd’hui, la question reste ouverte de savoir quelles formes pourrait prendre un sauvetage de l’IA et quelles en seraient les ramifications économiques et financières. Au niveau du secteur lui-même, on peut faire l’hypothèse que les entreprises néocloud et les fournisseurs de modèles fermés seront les plus touchés et pourraient faire les frais d’une restructuration qui profiterait d’abord à Microsoft, Amazon et Google – c’est-à-dire, à des acteurs qui interviennent aux différents niveaux du stack numérique. L’administration des États-Unis pourrait adopter diverses mesures de soutien au secteur telles qu’un accès à des conditions avantageuses de l’énergie, des prêts garantis et des prises de participation. Mais il est aussi à craindre que celles-ci s’accompagnent d’une pression accrue sur les autres pays afin de stabiliser les revenus de ses champions. Pour les pays européens, l’intensification de la dépendance aux services numériques étasuniens risque de se payer cher, mais une crise peut aussi ouvrir une fenêtre d’opportunité pour rebattre les cartes de la souveraineté numérique. Permettre la maîtrise de la production et de l’implémentation de l’IA suppose, d’une part, une politique industrielle associant protectionnisme numérique et internationalisme technologique Reclaiming digital sovereignty : A roadmap to build a digital stack for people and the planet », UCL InstituteforInnovation and Public Purpose , décembre 2024.'> 92 et, d’autre part, la création d’une régulation internationale. Cette crise devrait aussi conduire à une réévaluation critique des apports de l’IA et de la manière d’inscrire cette technologie dans des pratiques économiques et sociales respectueuses du travail, compatibles avec les processus démocratiques et en phase avec les contraintes écologiques. Enfin, sur le plan économique et financier, le choc récessif risque d’être brutal et le souffle puissant. La question reste de savoir dans quelle mesure les banques centrales pourront une nouvelle fois seconder les budgets publics pour prévenir une spirale dépressive, sans porter atteinte à la confiance dans la monnaie. En fonction de l’intensité du choc, le maintien de la centralité du dollar dans le système monétaire international pourrait ainsi être remis en cause. Nous nous trouvons au seuil d’une grande crise. Ses causes ne sont pas à rechercher dans les caractéristiques intrinsèques de l’IA comme technologie, mais dans les institutions héritées de la longue phase néolibérale. Celles-ci ont lâché la bride à l’innovation pour le profit et la plasticité financière. Elles ont entravé la formation d’un cadre international coopératif. Cette crise ne sera pas une surprise, tant la communauté financière semble l’attendre, mais sa maturation dépasse les enjeux économiques. La crise de l’IA sera politique. L’article La bulle et le contrôle est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Here’s what to expect from the ‘New Economy’ in the 2027 Budget
items.description: Government plans to invest approximately $10 billion over four years in what it calls a “New Economy”, with agriculture, manufacturing and job creation at the centre of the programme. A Finance Ministry document has provided an early indication of what to expect when Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson presents the budget on November 12. Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson It outlines seven pillars and proposes changes to government’s fiscal targets to create room for the investment. But much of what the programme seeks to achieve sounds familiar, particularly when viewed alongside the NDC’s flagship 24-Hour Economy policy. The first pillar is macroeconomic stability. Government’s position is that the gains made in stabilising the economy should now provide a foundation for investment, production and employment. The second focuses on commercial agriculture, agri-industry and agribusiness. The intention is to reduce dependence on imported food while creating jobs across farming, processing and related businesses. Energy sector reforms and investment form the third pillar, while critical minerals and value addition constitute the fourth, reflecting government’s ambition to retain more of the benefits from Ghana’s natural resources through domestic processing. The remaining three pillars cover cotton, textiles and garments; tourism, culture and creative arts; and the development of a pharmaceutical manufacturing hub. These are sectors with considerable potential to expand production and employment. However, the document does not yet identify the specific projects government intends to finance or how the proposed investment will be distributed among them. For instance, the pharmaceutical manufacturing pillar does not explain whether government intends to support existing manufacturers to expand, attract new producers or finance shared infrastructure. Similar questions arise around the proposed support for textiles and mineral processing. The 2027 Budget will need to provide greater clarity on these priorities. There is, however, a financing proposal. Government intends to commit 1.5% of GDP annually between 2027 and 2030, amounting to approximately $10 billion over the period. An additional 0.5% of GDP is expected to come from revenue measures, while the remaining fiscal space would be created by reducing the primary surplus target from 1.5% to 0.5% of GDP. In effect, government plans to mobilise additional revenue and create more room for productive investment while maintaining a primary surplus before interest payments. That could provide the resources needed to support the identified sectors. Whether it translates into the expected jobs and increased production, however, will depend on what the money finances and how the projects are implemented. It also raises a question about the place of the 24-Hour Economy in this new arrangement. The NDC’s manifesto described the policy as an intervention to encourage businesses and public institutions to operate in three shifts of eight hours each, boosting production and generating well-paying jobs. “The 24-Hour Economy policy aims to transform Ghana into an import-substitution and export-led economy,” it stated. Source: NDC 2024 Manifesto The manifesto promised cheaper electricity, tax incentives, financing support and improved security for participating businesses. Government would also use its purchasing power to support locally produced goods. Agro-processing, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, extractive industries and hospitality were among the sectors identified. Several of these priorities now feature prominently in the New Economy framework. The overlap is not particularly surprising. They are sectors Ghana needs to develop. But it raises an important question: what does the New Economy add to a programme government has already spent considerable time promoting? When the 24-Hour Economy blueprint was launched in July 2025, it had already expanded beyond the campaign emphasis on keeping businesses open for longer. As JoyNews Research explained at the time, the blueprint combined incentives for additional shifts with broader proposals for industrial parks, irrigation, energy and logistics. Its broader objective was to address the structural constraints preventing businesses from increasing production. So, is the New Economy now the framework through which government intends to finance and implement those proposals, or has it changed its approach? The fiscal strategy continues to mention the 24-Hour Economy alongside the New Economy and the Big Push infrastructure programme. It does not suggest that the earlier policy has formally been abandoned. There have also been some steps towards implementation. The 24-Hour Economy Authority Bill was signed into law in February 2026, while a downstream petroleum pilot was announced in May. What remains necessary and lacking, however, is a clear account of the results so far. President John Dramani Mahama After the extensive promotion of the 1-3-3 formula, government should explain how many businesses have introduced additional shifts, which incentives they have received and how many additional workers have been employed. Without that information, it is difficult to assess whether the New Economy builds on progress under the existing policy or reflects challenges in implementing it. There is also a broader question of policy continuity. The previous administration’s One District One Factory programme similarly sought to support private businesses, add value to local resources, replace imports and expand exports. Planting for Food and Jobs also aimed to increase agricultural production and employment while reducing dependence on food imports. The programmes differ in name and design, but many of the underlying challenges they seek to address remain the same. Factories still need affordable finance, reliable electricity, raw materials and customers. Farmers need access to inputs, storage, transport and reliable markets. These requirements do not change with a new policy name. Government will therefore need to demonstrate how its proposed investment addresses these constraints and what lessons it has drawn from previous programmes. It should also clarify whether existing projects will be incorporated into the New Economy and how their performance will be measured. The 2027 Budget presentation on November 12 should provide a clearer basis for that assessment. For now, the fiscal strategy sets out the sectors government wants to support and how it intends to create the fiscal space to finance them. The specific projects, delivery timelines and employment targets remain to be explained. Ultimately, those details will determine what is genuinely new about the New Economy and whether Ghanaians should expect a different outcome from another familiar promise of increased production and job creation.

items.title: No new Ghana Cards required under biometric verification law – NIA
items.description: The National Identification Authority (NIA) has assured Ghanaians that the implementation of the National Identity Register Amendment Regulation, 2026 (L.I. 2523), does not require the acquisition of new Ghana Cards or undergoing fresh biometric registration. Mr Williams Ampomah Emmanuel Darlas, Head of the NIA Corporate Affairs Directorate, said the regulation only changed how institutions and individuals verified identities, making biometric verification mandatory instead of relying solely on visual inspection of the cards. He said the existing Ghana Card remained the country’s official national identity document and would continue to be used for transactions requiring identity verification. Speaking at a press conference in Accra on Monday, Mr Darlas said the regulation sought to strengthen identity security, prevent impersonation and identity fraud, and protect personal information. He explained that biometric verification would rely on information captured during the initial registration, including fingerprints, iris details and facial features stored on the card’s embedded chip. He stressed that cardholders were not required to register their biometrics again or replace their existing cards. Cards issued in 2018, for instance, would remain valid until 2028, in accordance with the 10-year validity period, he said. The Authority would announce renewal arrangements when necessary, with measures being considered to prevent long queues, he added. Mr Darlas also clarified that the prohibition on photocopying, scanning and visually inspecting the Ghana Card did not prevent individuals from presenting their physical cards for biometric verification. He said telecommunications companies and some banks used a process known as match-on-card verification, which required customers to present their physical cards so their fingerprints could be matched against biometric information stored on the chip. “That is allowed. That is biometric verification, and that can only be done when you present the physical Ghana Card,” he said. Institutions connected to the NIA’s verification platform through an Application Programming Interface (API) could also verify customers using their Ghana Card numbers, he said. However, such institutions would violate the regulation if they subsequently relied on visual inspection, photocopying or scanning of the cards for identity verification. Mr Darlas said L.I. 2523 also applied to individuals under Regulations 9A and 9B, requiring biometric verification when conducting transactions with others where identity confirmation was necessary. He cited land transactions as an example, explaining that individuals could no longer rely solely on inspecting the Ghana Cards of parties involved to establish their identities. To facilitate compliance among individuals and small businesses without access to the NIA’s verification platform, the Authority had developed a mobile application. The application would enable users to confirm identities through a simple yes-or-no response without disclosing cardholders’ personal information, he said. He assured the public that measures had been put in place to protect information accessed through the application. Mr Darlas urged institutions and individuals to seek clarification from the NIA whenever they were uncertain about the application of the regulation. He also advised the public to report institutions that violated the regulation through the Biometric Verification Implementation Task Force hotline, 030-2999-309. The NIA would continue public education to ensure Ghanaians understood the new requirements and were not unnecessarily alarmed, he said.

items.title: Azma retorts as Salik remembers Parvez Elahi as ‘the best-ever CM’ in Punjab
items.description: LAHORE: The remarks by Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain declaring former Punjab chief minister Chaudhry Parvez Elahi as the province’s “best-ever chief minister” and his criticism of “unjust” distribution of development funds among the districts have caused unease within the Maryam Nawaz administration, drawing a sharp rebuttal from Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari, who advised the PML-Q leader not to “bite the hand that feeds him.” During a private television channel talk show on Monday, Salik lavished praise on Elahi, the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) president, crediting his 2002-07 tenure as Punjab chief executive with delivering development across the province without political or personal bias. “Former chief minister Chaudhry Parvez Elahi is the best-ever chief executive of Punjab,” he said, adding that Elahi had made a significant contribution to the province’s development and ensured that development initiatives were not dictated by political affiliations. The remarks carry particular political significance given the fractured relationship between the Chaudhry family and the PTI leadership. Salik, the younger son of PML-Q president Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, belongs to a family whose political loyalties have diverged sharply since the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in 2022 through a no-confidence vote. While Elahi and his son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, aligned themselves with the PTI, the Shujaat family chose to stand with the Sharifs. Salik’s elder brother, Shafay Hussain, is also part of the Maryam Nawaz cabinet in Punjab. PML-Q leader had also accused Punjab govt of discriminatory spending of public funds in districts Salik went beyond praising Elahi, and took a swipe at the present provincial administration, alleging that political considerations are increasingly shaping development priorities and influencing the allocation of public funds. He said he regularly heard complaints of corruption in Punjab, alleging that a disproportionate share of the province’s development budget was being channelled towards Lahore, while districts, like Gujrat, where government-backed candidates failed to win elections, were being sidelined in development planning. He also questioned lavish government spending, particularly the use of official aircraft, arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties. Officials using government aircraft, he said, should be required to demonstrate the tangible outcomes and public benefits of their trips. He further called for greater ministerial accountability, proposing that the federal as well as provincial ministers should be empowered to perform their duties, but also be held answerable for their performance. The criticism drew an immediate response from Punjab information minister Azma Bokhari, who sought to portray Salik’s outburst as a reaction to the denial of a personal favour, rather than a principled objection to the government’s policy. She alleged that his displeasure stemmed from a request for appointment of a deputy commissioner of his choice being turned down. “Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz does not appoint deputy commissioners at anyone’s recommendation. She makes decisions strictly on merit and in accordance with the government’s policy,” Bokhari said. Claiming that the chief minister had dismantled the culture of political patronage, personal preferences and recommendations, she maintained that there was no longer any space in Punjab for influential individuals seeking to secure government positions or administrative favours through political connections. “There is no room for land grabbers and strongmen in Punjab anymore. The practice of rewarding employees of political estates with government positions through recommendations has also come to an end. Salik Hussain should not bite the hand that feeds him,” she retorted. Rejecting Salik’s allegations of discriminatory development spending, Bokhari said Maryam Nawaz had ensured a transparent and equitable distribution of provincial resources, with development projects of a similar nature being launched in cities across Punjab. She also claimed that the sanitation model introduced in Lahore had been extended to rural areas, arguing that Punjab government was pursuing development beyond the provincial capital, rather than concentrating resources in one city. Responding to Salik’s criticism of official aircraft use, Bokhari said Ms Nawaz was the first Punjab chief minister to personally pay expenses incurred on the use of the government’s aeroplane. She also cited an allocation of Rs12 billion for development in Gujrat, describing it as an unprecedented investment in the city’s history. Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

items.title: Ghana envoy expects US police to identify killers of teenager shot dead in New York
items.description: Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, Victor Emmanuel Smith, says he expects American investigators to make progress in identifying those behind the fatal shooting of 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Javits Badu Nkansah Frimpong in New York. He has called for a comprehensive investigation to establish the motive for the killing and determine whether it was connected to allegations that Javits had been bullied at school. Mr Smith believes surveillance recordings from the area could provide important leads, even though reports indicate the attackers wore masks during the incident. He expressed confidence that the police would use available records and other evidence to track down those responsible. He also wants investigators to establish whether the suspects had any links to the student alleged to have bullied Javits, or to others involved in the incident. However, he cautioned against assuming that the alleged bully took part in the shooting without evidence. On Channel One TV on Monday, November 2, the Ambassador said the investigation must establish whether the killing was retaliation for the bullying incident and the punishment reportedly imposed on the student accused of bullying Javits. “I expect that they will conduct a thorough investigation to establish that the people who perpetrated that crime were the very people or connected with the people who did the bullying. There’s a need to establish that it wasn’t something else,” he said. He added that he was not in a position to determine whether the alleged bully was directly involved, noting that investigators would have to establish any connection through their inquiries and relevant school records. Meanwhile, residents of the Bronx neighbourhood where Javits was killed are expected to organise a vigil on Thursday, November 5, to remember the teenager and call for action against youth violence.

items.title: Queen Máxima to promote financial health during visit to Ghana
items.description: Queen Máxima of the Netherlands is in Ghana for a four-day visit aimed at improving the financial security of Ghanaians, amid concerns that millions of people with access to banking and mobile money services still struggle to manage their finances. Figures from the 2021 FinScope survey show that only 22 per cent of Ghanaian adults were financially healthy, while 44 per cent were managing to cope and another 34 per cent were financially vulnerable. This is despite significant progress in financial inclusion. The World Bank’s Global Findex 2025 report shows that more than 80 per cent of adults in Ghana had bank or mobile money accounts in 2024. Queen Máxima, who is visiting in her capacity as the United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Advocate for Financial Health, will engage government officials, financial institutions, farmers, traders and other stakeholders on ways to help Ghanaians save, manage debt and withstand financial emergencies. Her visit, which began on Monday, 2 nd November, will end on Thursday, 5 th November, 2026. The discussions will focus on improving access to affordable credit, agricultural financing, insurance and pensions, particularly for low-income households and workers in the informal sector. On Tuesday, 3 rd November 2026, Queen Máxima is scheduled to visit a farm and a fruit-processing factory in the Upper West Akim District, where she will interact with farmers and workers about the financial difficulties they face, including unstable incomes and limited access to insurance. She will also visit a hospital to learn how digital technology is helping patients manage chronic conditions such as diabetes and hypertension while reducing healthcare costs. In Accra, she will meet women traders at Makola Market to discuss how savings and loan products are helping them manage and expand their businesses. The Queen is expected to hold discussions with financial sector leaders at the Bank of Ghana on Wednesday, 4 th November 2026, before engaging the World Bank on improving pension coverage and long-term savings, particularly for informal sector workers. She will later travel to Kumasi to meet the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, his wife, Lady Julia Osei Tutu, and other traditional leaders. The visit will conclude on Thursday with high-level meetings involving President John Dramani Mahama, Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson, Food and Agriculture Minister Eric Opoku and Bank of Ghana Governor Dr. Johnson Asiama. The government is also expected to announce a new financial sector development strategy aimed at improving financial inclusion and the financial wellbeing of Ghanaians. The visit forms part of Queen Máxima’s global advocacy for financial systems that go beyond providing bank accounts to helping people meet daily expenses, cope with unexpected financial difficulties and build long-term financial security.

items.title: La factura de la luz se encarecerá en 2.000 millones al año si descarrila el decreto de centros de datos
items.description: En plena batalla por el futuro del despliegue digital en España, la factura eléctrica de los hogares y las empresas se enfrenta a una amenaza silenciosa de dimensiones milmillonarias. Permitir la conexión sin restricciones de los centros de datos proyectados para la próxima década disparará el recibo de la luz en cerca de 2.000 millones de euros cada año si el Gobierno finalmente deja sin aprobar la normativa que obliga a estas macroinstalaciones a respaldar su consumo con energía limpia. Esa es la contundente conclusión a la que llegan los expertos académicos del ámbito internacional de PyPSA Labs en una modelización del sistema eléctrico español: a falta de una regulación que imponga una sincronización horaria estricta entre consumo e inyección renovable, atender la demanda eléctrica de los servidores forzará a las centrales térmicas a quemar gas fósil de forma continuada, encareciendo el precio de la electricidad en el mercado mayorista en casi ocho euros por megavatio-hora (MWh) para todos los consumidores del país. items.title: ‎Bawumia calls for laws to protect workers from AI job losses
items.description: Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, Flagbearer of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), has called for legislation to protect workers from potential job losses arising from the growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). ‎He said although AI offered opportunities to improve productivity, efficiency and service delivery, its rapid advancement could threaten employment and workers’ income security. ‎Dr Bawumia made the call during an engagement with the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which focused on labour issues, economic transformation and the future of work. ‎He described AI as a “frightening prospect” for workers, noting that machines and software applications were increasingly capable of performing tasks traditionally undertaken by humans. ‎The former Vice-President said businesses worldwide were adopting automation to reduce operational costs and improve productivity, making several occupations vulnerable to technological disruption. ‎He said Ghana needed to take proactive measures to address the implications of AI on the labour market rather than remain a passive observer as the technology transformed industries. ‎Dr Bawumia stressed the need for a national strategy to ensure that the adoption of AI promoted economic growth without undermining workers’ livelihoods. ‎“Artificial Intelligence should be a tool to complement human labour and not a substitute for it,” he said. ‎Dr Bawumia proposed collaboration among the Government, organised labour, employers and technology experts to develop laws and regulations that would protect workers while encouraging innovation. ‎The proposed framework, he said, should provide for retraining, reskilling and continuous education to equip workers with the skills needed to remain relevant in an increasingly digital economy. ‎Dr Bawumia also encouraged labour unions to participate actively in national discussions on AI to ensure that workers had a voice in decisions affecting their employment and future. ‎He expressed concern that Africa’s youthful population could face increasing unemployment if technological advancement outpaced investment in human capital development. ‎Dr Bawumia said deliberate policies were needed to ensure that the benefits of AI were widely shared and did not deepen existing social and economic inequalities. ‎He expressed confidence that appropriate policies and legal safeguards would enable Ghana to harness the benefits of AI while protecting employment and preserving the dignity of work.

items.title: Mahama appoints Dr Hamid Kanyiti Salifu as Acting Deputy CEO of Student Loan Trust Fund
items.description: President John Mahama has appointed Dr Hamid Kanyiti Salifu as Acting Deputy Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Student Loan Trust Fund (SLTF) to strengthen the institution’s leadership and efforts to improve access to tertiary education financing. The Secretary to the President, Dr Callistus Mahama, communicated the appointment in a letter dated October 29, 2026. The letter stated that the appointment was made under Article 195(1) of the 1992 Constitution and the Student Loan Trust Fund Act, 2011 (Act 820), pending receipt of the constitutionally required advice of the Governing Board, in consultation with the Public Services Commission. Dr Salifu brings considerable experience in research, public administration, governance, and policy development to the position. Until his appointment, he served as a Resource Person for Research, Policy Development and Implementation at the African Centre for Parliamentary Affairs (ACEPA) in Accra. He previously worked as Research Officer and Head of Secretariat to former Minority Leader and current Member of Parliament for Tamale South, Hon. Haruna Iddrisu, during the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Parliaments. His responsibilities included coordinating the Minority Leader’s schedule, conducting parliamentary research and managing engagements between the office, public institutions and other stakeholders. Dr Salifu holds a PhD in Public Administration, Governance and Leadership from the Ghana Institute of Management and Public Administration (GIMPA). His doctoral research examined “Parliamentary Oversight and Executive Accountability in Ghana’s Democratic Governance under the Fourth Republic.” He also holds a Master’s degree in Development Management, specialising in International Development, from GIMPA, and a Bachelor of Science degree in Agribusiness (Management and Finance) from the University for Development Studies (UDS). Political and public service experience Dr. Salifu has also been actively involved in political organisation and electoral activities within the National Democratic Congress (NDC). His previous roles include serving as Collator of NDC presidential results for the Salaga South Constituency during the 2024 general elections, Elections Research Director of the NDC Youth Wing in the Northern Region and a member of the party’s regional campaign team during the 2016 elections. He also served as President of the Tertiary Education Institutions Network (TEIN) at the UDS Nyankpala Campus in the 2012 academic year. His earlier electoral experience includes serving as an NDC Regional Election Observer in the Northern Region during the 2004 and 2008 general elections and as a polling agent in Tamale during the 2000 elections. Beyond his parliamentary and political experience, Dr Salifu has an educational background, having previously taught at Bagabaga Demonstration Junior High School in Tamale. His classroom experience is expected to add perspective on students’ educational needs and the importance of accessible financing. Appointment comes amid student loan reforms Dr Salifu’s appointment comes as the Student Loan Trust Fund is expected to play an increasingly important role in the government’s efforts to improve access to tertiary education through sustainable student financing. In its 2024 manifesto, the NDC pledged to strengthen the Fund by reintroducing and deploying the Student Loan Trust Fund Plus (SLTFP), alongside reforms to the scholarship regime to provide continuing students with financial assistance. The party also promised to increase student loan amounts based on needs assessments and ensure timely disbursement of funds to beneficiaries. Under the leadership of its CEO, Dr Saajida Shiraz, the Fund has been spearheading efforts to advance reforms aimed at improving student financing. Dr Salifu is expected to support these initiatives by bringing his expertise in public governance, institutional management, research and policy development to the organisation. The Student Loan Trust Fund provides financial assistance to eligible Ghanaian students pursuing accredited undergraduate programmes at accredited tertiary institutions. Its mission is to transform lives through innovative student financing solutions by providing timely, accessible and affordable financial support. With a vision of promoting equitable access to quality tertiary education for all Ghanaians, the Fund remains a critical institution in efforts to reduce financial barriers to higher education. Dr Salifu’s appointment is therefore expected to strengthen the Fund’s leadership capacity as it works to improve its operations and deliver on the broader goal of making tertiary education more accessible to Ghanaian students.

items.title: Illegal mining threatening Ghana’s relations with neighbouring countries – Zanetor
items.description: The escalating illegal mining activities in Ghana are threatening the diplomatic relations between the country and its immediate neighbours in the West Africa sub-region. Dr. Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, Minister of Environment, Science, and Technology, who made this known, said the continued pollution of shared river systems by illegal mining activities in Ghana had been of grave concern to the immediate neighbours of Ghana. She cautioned that, the contamination of critical trans-boundary rivers, such as the Tano and Bia, which could cause toxic waters to spill across Ghana’s borders into Côte d’Ivoire, was elevating illegal mining from an environmental crisis to a severe threat to regional diplomacy and national security. Addressing a national conference on small-scale mining for Metropolitan, Municipal, and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) in Kumasi, Dr Agyeman-Rawlings stressed that the situation demanded immediate, coordinated action from the government, traditional leaders, security agencies, and local communities to address the illegal mining menace. She further noted that illegal mining was fueling broader security crises, warning that illicit proceeds from these activities were allegedly being used to finance violent extremism and terrorism in parts of the Sahel region. According to her, Ghana cannot afford to let complacency or silence render the nation complicit in activities that jeopardised security across the sub-region. Dr. Agyeman-Rawlings also warned that the destruction of forests and the toxic pollution of water bodies were severely undermining the country’s food security and exposing future generations to grave health hazards. She emphasised that Ghana must not prioritise gold production at the catastrophic expense of agriculture, water security, and other vital economic sectors. The minister cautioned that impending weather anomalies, compounded by the escalating impacts of climate change, could severely exacerbate the nation’s environmental challenges, particularly as rainfall patterns become increasingly erratic and temperatures rise. Highlighting the crucial role of forests, she stressed that trees were vital for regulating temperatures, sustaining local climates, and supporting life, warning that their reckless destruction through illegal mining would only accelerate environmental degradation. Citing scientific evidence, she pointed to research on the Odaw River in the Ashanti Region, which underscored the severe pollution driven by illicit mining activities. She also referenced assessments by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and its partners, which identified hazardous levels of toxic heavy metals, including mercury, lead, arsenic, and cadmium, in mining-impacted environments. Drawing on her background as a medical doctor, Dr Agyeman-Rawlings expressed profound concern over the public health implications of this pollution, particularly for children, pregnant women, and newborns. She warned that toxic runoff could jeopardise communities far beyond the immediate mining sites, noting that contaminated boreholes miles away often served as the primary drinking water sources for school children. The minister warned of catastrophic consequences for future generations if decisive and immediate measures were not implemented to halt this crisis. Turning her focus to local government authorities, she identified MMDCEs as pivotal frontline actors in the fight against illegal mining, asserting that this battle cannot be won through centralised directives from Accra alone. She reminded the MMDCEs of their statutory obligations under the Local Governance Act, 2016 (Act 936) and urged them to take the lead in the fight against the menace. Mr Armah Kofi Buah, Minister of Lands and Natural Resources, said the government implementing sweeping reforms in the mining sector to help decentralised licensing regimes to strengthen community participation and effectively address illegal mining activities.

items.title: Ghana Reference Rate falls to 10.01%, signalling further relief for borrowers
items.description: The Ghana Reference Rate (GRR), a key benchmark commercial banks use to price loans, has fallen to 10.01% for November 2026, signalling potential relief for borrowers. JoyBusiness calculations, based on the industry-approved formula and market data, put the rate below the 10.04% recorded in October. The latest movement extends the benchmark’s downward trend since September, although the November reduction is marginal at 0.03 percentage points. Market information obtained by JoyBusiness also indicates that some customers are securing consumer loans at rates of around 9%, below the GRR, as banks compete for business. Reasons and impact on cost of credit Market players attribute the decline largely to a marginal reduction in Treasury bill rates over the past month. The other components used to calculate the benchmark—the monetary policy rate and interbank rate—remained unchanged. The lower GRR could reduce borrowing costs for customers whose variable-rate loans are linked to the benchmark. Any adjustment will depend on their facilities’ terms and repricing schedules. Borrowers with such loans may have benefited from successive reductions since September. However, the GRR is a reference point, not the final interest rate charged to every customer. New borrowers could also benefit from the lower benchmark, depending on their credit profile and the bank’s pricing terms. Customers with fixed-rate loans are unlikely to see an automatic reduction in their repayments. Market participants say some individuals and businesses with strong credit histories are already securing single-digit lending rates. They also expect further easing as the government pursues measures to reduce the cost of credit. Tracking the decline and movement in 2026 The Ghana Reference Rate has moved in mixed directions this year. It stood at 11.71% in March before falling to 10.06% in April. It eased further to 10.03% in May and 10.02% in June. The benchmark then rose to 10.59% in July and 10.61% in August. It subsequently declined to 10.18% in September and 10.04% in October, before reaching the calculated November rate of 10.01%. The GRR provides a common reference point for loan pricing across the banking sector. Commercial banks use it alongside other pricing considerations to determine the interest rates on credit facilities.

items.title: Afenyo-Markin calls for stronger enforcement of audit findings across Africa
items.description: Alexander Afenyo-Markin, the Minority Leader in Parliament, has called on African countries to move beyond merely identifying financial irregularities and ensure the effective enforcement of audit recommendations to strengthen public accountability. He said public financial accountability could not be measured solely by the number of audit reports produced, officials questioned, or hearings conducted, but by the corrective actions taken, recovery of public funds, and sanctions imposed where wrongdoing had been established. In an address at the opening of the Sixth Conference and General Meeting of the African Organisation of Public Accounts Committees (AFROPAC) in Accra on Monday, Mr Afenyo-Markin said the continent could not continue to “audit the same failures year after year without holding anyone accountable.” The conference, being attended by Public Accounts Committee members, parliamentary officials, auditors and governance experts from across Africa, is on the theme: “Oversight for Resilience: Strengthening Public Accounts Committees for Accountability in a Changing Financial Landscape.” Quoting a 2017 Supreme Court ruling in the case of Occupy Ghana vs. Attorney-General, the Minority Leader said the protection of public resources required actionable enforcement, integrity, and statutory authority. He noted that weak financial accountability had real-life consequences for citizens, including inadequate healthcare facilities, poor educational infrastructure, unfinished roads, and limited access to essential public services. “We are living through a period of intense global and continental economic turbulence. African nations are facing severe macroeconomic shocks, expanding debt obligations, inflationary pressures and shrinking fiscal space,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin observed that citizens were becoming increasingly informed and demanding greater transparency in the management of public resources. He noted that the growing public scrutiny placed a greater responsibility on institutions tasked with safeguarding state resources and ensuring value for money. The Minority Leader identified the implementation of audit recommendations as one of the most significant challenges confronting public financial management systems across the continent. “Year after year, audit reports reveal irregular expenditures, procurement breaches, weaknesses in revenue collection and deficiencies in public asset management, yet the key question remains: what happens after the hearings have ended?” he asked. To address the challenge, Mr Afenyo-Markin proposed five structural reforms to strengthen Public Accounts Committees across Africa. These involved: the institutionalisation of real-time and concurrent oversight mechanisms, enhancing forensic and digital auditing capabilities of committee secretariats, statutory tracking and enforcement of audit recommendations, increased scrutiny of sovereign debt and illicit financial flows, and stronger inter-parliamentary intelligence-sharing arrangements. He said evolving financial systems, including digital public financial management platforms, public-private partnerships, sovereign debt instruments and cross-border financial transactions, required oversight institutions to adopt modern approaches. “If our committees remain anchored in analogue, delayed oversight mechanisms, our democratic demand for accountability will fail,” he stated. Mr Afenyo-Markin also called for increased collaboration among African legislatures through AFROPAC to share best practices and develop common approaches to addressing public financial management challenges. He noted that while constitutional arrangements differed across countries, many of the accountability challenges confronting African parliaments were similar. The Minority Leader further stressed that financial accountability should not depend on whether a political party was in government or opposition. “Public financial accountability must never become a principle that we defend only when we occupy the opposition benches and conveniently disregard when entrusted with government power,” he said. He urged both majority and minority lawmakers to approach oversight responsibilities with fairness, diligence and fidelity to evidence. Mr Afenyo-Markin concluded by urging delegates to use the conference as an opportunity to renew their commitment to strong parliamentary oversight and effective protection of public resources. “The strength of African parliaments will not be measured by the number of bills they pass, but by the vigilance with which they guard the public purse,” he said.
