items.title: Puente se enfrenta a su comparecencia clave con un plan de medidas para reforzar la seguridad de los trenes
items.description: El Gobierno tiene este martes jornada política decisiva para ver cómo es capaz de gestionar la grave crisis de credibilidad provocada por el segundo accidente mortal en nueve meses en la alta velocidad española. Óscar Puente, el ministro de Transportes, presentará por la mañana en el Consejo de Ministros un paquete de medidas con dos patas: una, la de las ayudas a las víctimas, que ya apuntó Pedro Sánchez este martes en su intervención en el foro World in Progress (WIP) organizado por el Grupo PRISA en Barcelona, y otra, la de las mejoras en seguridad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las centrales sindicales del ferrocarril se plantean una fuerte movilización para acelerar refuerzos en la seguridad
items.description: Los sindicatos con representación en el sector ferroviario vuelven a plantearse una fuerte movilización —“sin precedentes”, apuntan algunas fuentes— para exigir medidas de apuntalamiento de la seguridad en las redes convencional y de alta velocidad. El potente colectivo de maquinistas SEMAF , con unos 6.500 afiliados entre los 7.000 conductores de trenes que se contabilizan en el país, tomó una primera decisión tras el siniestro del pasado miércoles 28 de octubre en Urda : mantener la huelga del día después, 29, y convocar nuevos paros para el 10 y 12 de noviembre, el día anterior y la jornada posterior a la huelga general. Pese a los servicios mínimos que impone el Ministerio de Transportes, se esperan tres días de cierta convulsión en los servicios de tren. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Seguridad ferroviaria: cuando el error humano es un síntoma del sistema
items.description: El accidente de Urda del 28 de octubre de 2026, con al menos 69 fallecidos, es el segundo siniestro mortal de la alta velocidad española en diez meses. La causa inmediata apunta a un error humano: tras caer el LZB, el Centro de Control de Adif ordenó reanudar la marcha normal cuando había un tren detenido en la vía. Atribuir la tragedia solo a esa decisión elude la pregunta fundamental: ¿por qué el sistema permitió que un error previsible tuviera consecuencias letales? Seguir leyendo

items.title: Rafael, uno de los pasajeros del primer vagón del AVE, despierta de la sedación
items.description: Carmen Marcos y Rafael Hernández, ambos de 55 años, se conocieron en el instituto Fortuny de Madrid. Son novios desde los 16, en una relación que empezó en el aula. Y de cuyo amor nacieron Inés y Carmen. Ellas tres tienen hoy los ojos henchidos de felicidad. Ya no hay lágrimas. Están sentadas en la sala de espera de la Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos (UCI) del Hospital Universitario de Toledo, uno de los centros sanitarios donde los heridos del accidente de Urda fueron derivados . El miércoles se enteraron de que el tren en el que iba su marido y padre había embestido otro convoy. Rafael era pasajero en el primer vagón del AVE —el número 8—, uno de los más afectados y que se llevó por delante al Iryo. Desde entonces hasta este domingo por la tarde, Rafael había estado sedado con heridas muy graves. Pese al complicadísimo pronóstico y la asfixiante espera que arrancó el miércoles, ellas siempre confiaron en que saldría adelante. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los hospitales de Castilla-La Mancha dejan atrás los días a la carrera por el accidente de Urda
items.description: Las grúas, los operarios y las máquinas trabajaban este lunes a toda velocidad , tal y como había ordenado la jueza que instruye el caso, Aristea Afroditi Ortiz. Lo hicieron durante toda la noche, cuando se movieron los vagones del AVE, y siguieron con los primeros rayos del sol, cuando comenzaron a verse los coches siniestrados colgados como gigantescas piñatas. Al caer la tarde, las grúas se habían llevado dos de los cuatro vagones del tren Iryo y solo quedaban otros dos sobre la vía, que más tarde ya no estaban. Todos los coches retirados de la zona cero de Urda serán trasladados a una zona custodiada por la autoridad judicial, confirmó la Guardia Civil. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Por qué la segunda oleada de ‘hackeos’ a las neveras en supermercados avisa de los riesgos que vienen
items.description: Decenas de supermercados de al menos siete países europeos amanecieron este lunes con parte de su género estropeado. Un ciberataque subió la temperatura de las cámaras frigoríficas de varios establecimientos, en algunos casos hasta los 50 grados, echando a perder productos frescos y congelados. Los países más afectados fueron Bélgica y Suecia, pero también se registraron problemas en Luxemburgo, Países Bajos, Irlanda, Estonia y Finlandia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: James Ellis Ford, de producir a Fontaines D.C. y Depeche Mode a grabar con Olivia Rodrigo desde el hospital por una leucemia: “Nunca me permití pensar que iba a morir”
items.description: El inglés James Ellis Ford (Leek, 47 años) se encontraba en la cima de su carrera, grabando con las bandas más prestigiosas de Reino Unido y Estados Unidos; pero pasó de hacerlo en los mejores estudios de todo el planeta a coordinar grabaciones desde una cama del hospital, e incluso grabar un disco propio. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Saqueos: apetito por la destrucción... y por las marcas
items.description: El viernes al anochecer, bajando por la calle Fuencarral, algunas tiendas colocaban paneles en sus ventanales por miedo a los saqueos que se planeaban por las redes. Otro retazo de ciencia ficción distópica que se añade a nuestra vida cotidiana. Al ver a los operarios afanarse en las escaleras de tijera y los taladros, me sentí inmerso en las películas de La purga , que relatan el horror de unos Estados Unidos ficticios en los que, un día al año, se suspende el imperio de la ley y todo está permitido. El día de la purga puedes romper lo que quieras, puedes matar a quien quieras, no hay consecuencias. Una parte de la ciudadanía se encastilla en casa, otra sale con machetes, bates, motosierras y máscaras terroríficas. Halloween contribuía este finde a la ambientación: entre los comercios atrincherados pululaban calaveras y diablitos buscando algún lugar donde tomar algo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Felipe VI se enfrenta al reto de evitar que los insultos de Milei dinamiten la cumbre de Madrid
items.description: Felipe VI se enfrenta en la XXX Cumbre Iberoamericana que se celebra este miércoles y jueves en Madrid a su más difícil reto internacional desde que accedió al trono hace más de 12 años. Como anfitrión de una cita a la que han sido invitados los mandatarios de los 22 países de habla española y portuguesa de Europa y América, al Rey le corresponde presidir la cumbre y ordenar los debates de los jefes de Estado y de Gobierno. Una tarea nada fácil, reconocen fuentes de la organización, en un foro en el que el presidente argentino Javier Milei coincidirá con el español Pedro Sánchez, a quien hace menos de dos semanas calificaba en Madrid de “impresentable dictador”, “corrupto” y “autoritario”. Si el mandatario argentino hace gala de su característica incontinencia verbal, a Felipe VI no le quedaría más remedio que retirarle la palabra, advierten las fuentes consultadas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Del miedo a la ultraderecha al regreso a los derechos básicos: Frente Amplio y Podemos afinan sus estrategias para el 29-N tras el accidente
items.description: La tragedia ferroviaria de Urda ha obligado a adaptar el diseño de las campañas electorales para el 29-N. A 10 días del arranque de la contienda, el espacio a la izquierda del PSOE, dividido en las papeletas de Frente Amplio y Podemos, se enfrenta a las urnas en un contexto extremadamente duro, con el ánimo del electorado muy golpeado por el suceso y las dudas generadas sobre el sistema y la responsabilidad del Gobierno en el segundo accidente de trenes en nueve meses, un ángulo que abordará la comparecencia de Óscar Puente este martes en la Diputación Permanente del Congreso. Tras unos días de relativo silencio, las campañas de ambos hablarán mucho de vivienda y denunciarán el riesgo de la llegada de PP y Vox al poder. A falta de más detalles, la candidatura que lidera Irene Montero en estas generales planea una gira de varios actos con Gabriel Rufián; uno de ellos en Alicante, y Pablo Fernández, número tres del partido, ejercerá de director de campaña. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Zapatero buscará dar un nuevo valor a las joyas con otra pericial
items.description: José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero buscará otra cifra para sus joyas. El expresidente quiere solicitar al juez de la Audiencia Nacional que le mantiene investigado, José Luis Calama, que permita a un perito de parte realizar una tasación alternativa para rebajar la cifra millonaria que, hasta ahora, dos casas de joyas distintas han peritado, según explican fuentes del entorno del que fuera líder socialista. El magistrado, que ha cuestionado la versión de que se tratara de un regalo del monarca saudí fallecido Abdalá Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud y se ha negado a emitir una petición de información a Arabia Saudí para corroborar este extremo, debe todavía pronunciarse sobre si imputar al expresidente por delito de malversación tras haberse quedado con unas piezas que, supuestamente, debían ser del erario público. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Gobierno obliga a los ayuntamientos a multar ya a los coches contaminantes en las zonas de bajas emisiones
items.description: El Consejo de Ministros aprobará previsiblemente este martes un real decreto para poner coto a las zonas de bajas emisiones fake , aquellas que se ponen en marcha como medida cosmética para cumplir la ley, pero que no reducen el tránsito ni la contaminación. El texto del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica exige a los 151 ayuntamientos de más de 50.000 habitantes obligados a instaurar una de estas áreas comunicar la entrada en vigor de las restricciones de acceso, circulación y estacionamiento de vehículos contaminantes. Además, conmina a los ayuntamientos a que multen ya a los infractores, “sin recurrir a sistemas transitorios que demoren su efectividad”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Universidad Rey Juan Carlos necesita un préstamo de 40 millones de Ayuso para no colapsar
items.description: El rector de la Universidad Rey Juan Carlos (URJC), Abraham Duarte, anunció el pasado viernes a sus trabajadores y estudiantes durante el Consejo de Gobierno que “valora” pedir un préstamo de en torno a 40 millones de euros al Gobierno de Isabel Díaz Ayuso para evitar su colapso económico, una notificación que el rectorado ha reconocido a EL PAÍS. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las claves de la crisis del Tribunal Constitucional en Polonia: forcejeos, acusaciones de golpe de Estado y guerra política
items.description: El Tribunal Constitucional (TC) de Polonia se ha convertido en un campo de batalla político y judicial. La suspensión del presidente y vicepresidente del tribunal el pasado viernes desencadenó un nuevo episodio convulso en una crisis que dura más de una década. Un bando acusa al otro de golpe de Estado, mientras el otro considera delictiva la actuación del presidente, Karol Nawrocki. Estas son las claves para no perderse en lo que el exjuez del Constitucional Miroslaw Wyrzykowski llama con humor “una telenovela brasileña”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Exiliados rusos en Occidente: entre el miedo y la sospecha
items.description: La invasión a gran escala de Ucrania lanzada por Rusia en 2022 alimenta el éxodo de ciudadanos rusos que rechazan someterse a la política militarista de Vladímir Putin. Los que emigran a Europa para protegerse del autoritarismo del Kremlin forman un conjunto variopinto: en él hay cualificados informáticos, prestigiosos intelectuales, estudiantes, jóvenes temerosos de la movilización, periodistas y activistas políticos prófugos de la justicia rusa. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Jeff Koons, el artista vivo más cotizado: “Se me asocia con cosas muy valiosas, pero nunca pienso en el precio”
items.description: Hay una idea en el budismo mahāyāna que dice que todo el universo puede encapsularse en el objeto más insignificante. Una de sus formulaciones es la red de Indra: el universo es una red de joyas, cada una de las cuales refleja a todas las demás. Dado que el artista Jeff Koons (York, Pensilvania, 71 años) afirma estar muy interesado por la filosofía oriental y que, además, sus objetos más conocidos son tan relucientes y llamativos como un rubí, no parece descabellado intentar explicar todo su mundo a través de una figura. De un perrito, concretamente. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Los parques infantiles de caucho reciclado son peligrosos para los niños?
items.description: Una campaña de Ecologistas en Acción ha puesto sobre la mesa el tema de los parques infantiles fabricados con caucho reciclado y sus posibles riesgos para los más pequeños, mientras el sector apunta que cumplen la legalidad y que ningún organismo europeo ha determinado que sean inseguros. items.title: El zar que se negó a subir en ascensor (o cómo este invento acabó con las viejas jerarquías para crear unas nuevas)
items.description: El ascensor es un invento que tiene ya unos dos mil años. En algunas de las insulae romanas –edificios de apartamentos que podían alcanzar las ocho plantas– ya había ascensores tirados por fuerza de sangre. Pero el ascensor moderno, el mecánico, el que existe gracias al freno de seguridad que ideó Elisha Otis, apenas llega al siglo y medio de antigüedad, que parece poca cosa (de ahí el “apenas”), pero que es una eternidad en términos de transformación de la ciudad. Sin el ascensor la gente en silla de ruedas estaría condenada a vivir en el plano horizontal, sin el ascensor no habría rascacielos ni torres de comunicaciones ni grúas que construyeran esas torres. Sin el ascensor el mundo sería otro, y nosotros lo usamos cada día como si nada, entramos en uno cada día, pulsamos los botones cada día y cada día nos peleamos con nuestros hijos pequeños para que no pulsen todos los botones a la vez. El ascensor es paisaje cotidiano. Pero no siempre fue así. Al principio, hubo muchas personas que se negaron a usarlos, a veces por miedo, a veces, como en el caso del zar Nicolas II, los consideraban una amenaza existencial para su estatus. Siéntate, que te voy a contar una historia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: EE UU ya es un Estado artificial, posliterario y fascista
items.description: La democracia estadounidense está en trance de extinción, dinamitada desde dentro por las instituciones sobre las que supuestamente se sustentaba. No cabe duda de que las próximas midterms serán importantes, pero por desgracia los problemas de fondo del país no van a desaparecer. Con Donald Trump se ha consolidado la peor imagen que Estados Unidos ha ofrecido al mundo desde su fundación hace 250 años, tras instaurar una forma de democracia considerada modélica en distintos momentos de la historia por figuras como Tocqueville, Walt Whitman, o Hannah Arendt. En los más de 40 años que llevo viviendo aquí he sido testigo del deterioro gradual que la democracia norteamericana ha ido experimentando hasta desembocar en lo que no cabe caracterizar más que como fascismo. Quien primero me hizo tomar conciencia de ello fue Norman Mailer, durante una entrevista concedida a este periódico con motivo de la publicación de Por qué estamos en guerra cuando, basándose en falsedades, el Gobierno de Estados Unidos decidió invadir Irak en marzo de 2003. “Bush es el presidente más estúpido que hemos tenido”, rezaba el titular de la entrevista. Habría sido interesante ver qué diría hoy Mailer de quien decidió embarcar gratuitamente a su país en la guerra de Irán, que tan graves consecuencias está teniendo para la estabilidad del orden internacional. Lo más llamativo de las declaraciones de Mailer es la razón por la que creía que el Gobierno de su país actuó de la manera en que lo hizo: “En Estados Unidos la democracia está siendo sometida a un proceso de acoso y derribo. Estamos viviendo una situación de prefascismo. Todavía no somos un país fascista, pero podría ocurrir pronto”, afirmó entonces. El tiempo no ha hecho más que darle la razón. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Without the media, there is no democracy – Major (rtd) Don-Chebe
items.description: Major (rtd) Albert Don-Chebe, former Director-General of the Ghana Broadcasting Corporation (GBC), has described the media as the foundation of democracy because it safeguards and promotes democratic governance and accountability. “For those of us for whom free speech is so critical, we understand that without the media, there is no democracy, and the health of any democracy can be determined from how free the media in that society is”, he explained. Major Don-Chebe said this at the second edition of the Upper West Regional Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Awards ceremony held in Wa at the weekend. The ceremony, held under the theme “Upholding Media Excellence: Promoting Ethical Journalism, Accountability, and Regional Development”, recognised seven outstanding journalists and media practitioners for their contributions to the profession’s growth. They were: Philip Tengzu of the Ghana News Agency; Ibrahim Muniru, Radio Mak; Ayamga Bawa Fatawu, a Freelance Journalist; Rafiq Nungor Adam, Channel 247; Ibrahim Abubakari Wangara, Media General; Gladys Wein Kitty, GBC Radio Upper West; and Kwadwo Baffoe Donkor of Daily Graphic. Major Don-Chebe, who chaired the event, expressed concern about Ghana’s ranking on the media freedom index, but added that media freedom in the country was gradually improving. “I am looking forward to us coming down to the high heights that we achieved some ten years or so ago when we were counted among the first 25 countries with the freest media in the world”, he stated. He said initiatives such as the awards ceremony provided an important platform to appreciate, acknowledge and motivate journalists to remain committed to their professional responsibilities. Mr Dominic Hlordzi, the General Secretary of the GJA, who represented the GJA President at the event, observed that awards ceremonies were important instruments for promoting excellence, encouraging healthy competition and raising professional standards within the media. He said recognising outstanding journalists was consistent with the Association’s aim of promoting professionalism and rewarding responsible, ethical, impactful and development-oriented journalism and commended the leadership of the Association in the region for the initiative. Mr Hlordzi stressed the need for journalism to transcend reporting events to highlighting the concerns, aspirations and development priorities of communities. He urged journalists in the region to intensify reportage on critical sectors, including education, healthcare, agriculture, infrastructure, sanitation, youth development and tourism, to draw national attention to the region’s development needs and opportunities. “Let us tell the stories that matter, expose the challenges that require urgent attention and spotlight initiatives that are transforming lives”, Mr Hlordzi indicated. He further called on journalists to use their platforms to amplify the concerns of underrepresented communities and ensure that duty-bearers addressed issues affecting their welfare.

items.title: Richmond Adu-Poku: Too many shows, too little December
items.description: It is October 2026, and somewhere in Accra, an event organiseris probably staring at a calendar, rubbing their hands together and thinking, “December will be massive!” Somewhere else, an artiste is planning a concert, another is booking a venue, and a third is announcing a festival. Meanwhile, the fan is checking their bank balance and wondering whether enjoying Christmas requires a second job. Welcome to Detty December, Ghana’s annual celebration of music, culture, tourism and entertainment, where the fun is unlimited, the invitations are endless, and the money in your pocket has a very different opinion. From concerts and music festivals to raves, beach parties, comedy shows, religious gatherings, award ceremonies and celebrity-hosted parties, December has become the entertainment industry’s favourite playground. Accra, in particular, transforms into a giant stage, attracting returning diaspora visitors, tourists and locals eager to end the year on a high note. It is exciting, no doubt. But beneath the glitter, fireworks and Instagram stories lies an uncomfortable question: Are we giving fans more entertainment, or simply giving them more decisions to regret? Too limited time and money The problem with Detty December is no longer a shortage of events, but the shortage of time, money and energy to enjoy them. With artistes scheduling concerts on the same dates, fans are forced to choose between their favourites, while Accra traffic makes attending multiple shows a near-impossible mission. Unfortunately, Ghana has no universal holiday or vacation calendar that gives everyone a month off to enjoy the festivities. Most people work hard throughout the year, only to find their December savings competing with concert tickets, transport, food, outfits and family obligations. Rising ticket prices and overlapping events make the season even more demanding. While the diaspora market brings valuable spending power, its presence does not guarantee attendance at every show. Local fans remain the backbone of the industry and should not be treated as an endless supply of money, time and energy. Ultimately, when everyone fights for the same audience, the industry risks exhausting the very people it depends on. Artistes, Please Consider the Artistes There are 12 months in a year. January, February, March and the others have not resigned from the entertainment industry. Yet, December has become the default month for artistes who want to headline their own concerts, unveil projects or end the year with a grand statement. The reasoning is understandable. The diaspora returns, the atmosphere is festive, and consumers are more willing to spend on experiences. But when everyone chases the same opportunity, the opportunity becomes overcrowded. Artistes must begin to consider their colleagues, not just their own event budgets. Two artistes with overlapping audiences scheduling major concerts on the same night may divide demand instead of expanding it. The result could be lower attendance, reduced spending per event and fans who leave disappointed because they could not support everyone. A successful concert calendar should encourage participation, not force fans into an entertainment version of Sophie’s Choice. And let us not forget the media. Smaller radio stations, online platforms and entertainment publications often operate with limited staff and budgets. When several major events happen simultaneously, comprehensive coverage becomes almost impossible. Someone must miss out, whether it is the journalist, the audience or the event itself. December Is Not the Only Month Worth Celebrating The solution is not to cancel Detty December. That would be like asking Ghana to celebrate Christmas quietly. The solution is to distribute the excitement. Artistes and promoters should explore a more balanced annual event calendar, with major concerts spread across the other 11 months. February could host a lovers’ concert. April could welcome a music festival. June could celebrate live bands and cultural music. August could become a destination for outdoor entertainment. September and October could accommodate album concerts and intimate fan experiences. These are examples, not rigid prescriptions. The point is to build a year-round entertainment economy rather than a one-month traffic jam. Industry stakeholders, including artistes, managers, promoters, venues, tourism authorities and media organisations, should collaborate on an annual event calendar. Such coordination would help identify major clashes, improve publicity, support ticket sales and give audiences more opportunities to attend. Promoters should also explore partnerships and shared programming where appropriate, particularly when events can complement rather than compete with one another. Most importantly, artistes should understand that finishing the year successfully does not require staging a personal concert. Releasing a great song, rewarding loyal fans, supporting a charitable cause, hosting a smaller appreciation event or delivering memorable performances at other people’s shows can be equally meaningful. Give the Fans a Fighting Chance There is also a responsibility to improve the concert experience itself. Reasonable ticket pricing, reliable start times, clear communication and genuine value for money are essential. Fans should not have to choose between competing concerts only to arrive at their preferred event and wait three hours for the headliner. The industry must remember that attendance is not merely a number on a ticketing dashboard. It represents a person who has invested money, time and expectation into an experience. A healthier event calendar could encourage fans to attend more shows throughout the year, help promoters build sustainable brands and give artistes more room to connect with their audiences. The Final Chorus December should be a celebration, not an examination in financial discipline, time management and emotional compromise. Ghana’s entertainment industry has an opportunity in 2026 to move beyond the obsession with one festive month and build a culture of consistent live entertainment. The objective should be to create more opportunities for artistes, better business for promoters, stronger coverage for the media and, above all, more satisfying experiences for fans. The audience cannot be in two places at once. The wallet cannot be stretched indefinitely. And the calendar, unfortunately, has refused to add extra days simply because our favourite artistes want to headline. Dear artistes and promoters, the fans have supported you since January. Consider giving them more opportunities to see you without forcing them to choose between you and another artiste they love. December is special, but it is not the only month with a stage. Spread the shows, share the spotlight and give the fans room to breathe.

items.title: Ligue1: l'OM rend hommage à Amine Harit, "porteur d'une dynamique positive"
items.description: L'entraineur de l'Olympique de Marseille, Bruno Genesio, a rendu un hommage appuyé à l'international marocain Amine Harit, affirmant que « par son énergie communicative, le milieu offensif apporte une dynamique positive à ses partenaires ». « Harit a de la confiance et montre l’étendue de son talent sur les un contre un. Il a de l’enthousiasme qu'il transmet aux autres et j’en suis content », a-t-il déclaré à l'issue de la victoire des Marseillais dimanche à domicile contre Toulouse (2-0). Le technicien français s'est déclaré agréablement surpris par le rôle du joueur, « même s'il n'évolue pas à son poste » , soulignant qu'il « apprécie sa capacité de transmettre de l’enthousiasme à ses coéquipiers ». Aligné en tant qu'ailier depuis le début de la saison, Amine Harit (29 ans) a su répondre aux attentes de l’entraîneur en apportant de la percussion et de la spontanéité dans le jeu marseillais. Il a été notamment l'un des artisans des quatre victoires de rang remportées en Ligue 1, une performance permettant au club de remonter en sixième position au classement et de viser, désormais, une place dans les prochaines compétitions européennes. Face à Toulouse FC dimanche soir, l'ailier n'a eu besoin que de deux minutes pour faire la différence. Parfaitement lancé en profondeur par Amine Gouiri, Harit a ouvert le score en trompant Guillaume Restes d’un extérieur du pied droit subtil. L'OM a ensuite doublé la mise grâce à la 25e minute, avant de préserver son avantage en dépit d’une seconde période plus compliquée. Auteur de son troisième but de la saison en Ligue 1, après ses réalisations contre Troyes et Angers, l’international marocain confirme son retour en forme et remporte le trophée d’homme du match. Devant les médias à l'issue de la rencontre, le joueur marocain a mis en avant l'importance de voir le jeu collectif prendre le dessus et de gagner en confiance pour aborder les prochaines échéances avec sérénité et concentration. The post Ligue1: l'OM rend hommage à Amine Harit, "porteur d'une dynamique positive" appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Cape Coast Court Complex falls silent as JUSAG strike locks out litigants
items.description: An unusual, deafening silence hung over the Cape Coast Court Complex on Monday, as the Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) nationwide strike brought judicial activities in the Central Regional capital to a standstill. When the Ghana News Agency (GNA) visited the facility at about 0800 hours, the three main entrances to the court complex were locked with red bands tied across the gates to signal that the facility was closed to staff, lawyers, litigants and the general public. Some security personnel were seen hovering on the premises, apparently to prevent unauthorised entry. The usual bustle of a working court day, lawyers moving between registries, litigants waiting for their cases, clerks attending to files, and security officers directing visitors, was conspicuously absent. JUSAG declared an indefinite strike effective Monday, November 2, after the government failed to approve the Judicial Council’s recommendations on the 2026 salary review for Judicial Service staff. The Association had demanded approval of the recommendations by the end of October and payment of the revised salaries in November, together with arrears covering January to October 2026. It said the delay followed months of engagement since December 2025, when it submitted proposals for the review under Article 149 of the 1992 Constitution and the relevant Judicial Service regulations. JUSAG argued that although the Judicial Council had completed its work and submitted its advice, it had not received the necessary approval and implementation, leaving members frustrated and demoralised. The industrial action has affected court operations nationwide, with several courts, including superior and lower courts, forced to close or restrict public access. At the Cape Coast Court Complex, the closure left some litigants and members of the public stranded outside, unsure when their matters would be heard. Among them was a 75-year-old man who had travelled from Dunkwa-on-Offin for a chieftaincy case adjourned to Monday, November 02. The elderly man told the GNA that although he had heard announcements about the impending strike, he was uncertain about it. He appealed to the government and JUSAG to resolve their differences quickly to prevent innocent citizens from suffering the consequences of the impasse. The strike also affected traders, particularly egg sellers and other vendors who usually depend on the daily human traffic around the court complex for their livelihood. Some traders expressed disappointment that the closure would deprive them of customers. “On a normal court day, people buy eggs, water and food here. Today, I have been sitting here for hours without selling. This strike will affect us,” she said. The traders called for an early resolution of the disagreement between JUSAG and the government, saying the prolonged closure of the courts would worsen their economic hardships. Some affected litigants appealed to the government to prioritise the welfare and working conditions of judicial staff to ensure the smooth administration of justice.

items.title: Mahama Ayariga warns MMDCEs, Regional Ministers against turning blind eye to galamsey
items.description: The Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, has warned Regional Ministers and Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) that they cannot escape responsibility for illegal mining under their watch. He says public officials who witness galamsey operations in their jurisdictions but fail to intervene are contributing to the problem, even if they are not directly involved in the mining. Speaking at the National Conference for Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives on Illegal Small-Scale Mining in Kumasi, Mr Ayariga insisted that the campaign against galamsey must become a shared responsibility rather than being left to the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources. “If you are not part of the problem, you must be part of the solution. And it is not only when you are directly, actively involved in mining that you are part of the problem. You can be part of the problem because you have seen people actively mining and you have looked the other way,” he said. He argued that Regional Ministers and MMDCEs are strategically positioned to identify and respond to illegal mining because they live and work within the communities where the activities occur. Mr Ayariga said the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, should not be expected to carry the entire burden of the campaign while local authorities fail to act on developments within their administrative areas. “The Minister for Lands and Natural Resources does not sleep in our districts. His office is in Accra. He can do so much to deal with the problem. But we, as MMDCEs and Regional Ministers, sleep in the districts where the action takes place, and there is so much that we can also do to fix the problem,” he stated. He said local government authorities must demonstrate greater commitment to monitoring mining activities and ensuring that illegal operations are not allowed to continue unchecked in their jurisdictions.

Economista y política, fue la primera mujer en ocupar la Secretaría Iberoamericana (2014-2021) , y la Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre Comercio y Desarrollo (UNCTAD) . UN reports warn of large-scale damage to Earth’s ice from climate change
items.description: PARIS: Exceeding 1.5C of global warming will have “irreversible” consequences for glaciers, sea ice and the Earth’s frozen regions, two UN reports warned on Monday, calling for urgent action. The landmark 2015 Paris Agreement commits the world to limiting warming to well below 2C and pursuing efforts to hold it at 1.5C to try to avoid the worst effects of climate change. One of the reports said overshooting the 1.5C target “will bring large-scale and in many cases irreversible impacts” for the cryosphere — Earth’s ice in all its forms. Melting of glaciers and sea ice, the thawing of permafrost and the accelerating rise in sea levels, will have widespread repercussions, from flooding to water shortages. Some of the effects of the rise in temperature are already visible, such as the 20-percent loss in glacial mass in Switzerland. But even if the 1.5C target remains relevant, it is already too high for the cryosphere, as current levels of warming were “already unsafe” for the Arctic, Antarctic, mountain glaciers and polar oceans, the UN warned. “Although returning to 1.5 C will slow ice loss, a truly ‘safe’ temperature for Earth’s ice is now thought to be closer to 1C or even below over the coming centuries,” it added. Global warming has already reached 1.37C above pre-industrial levels and according to the European Copernicus network, the 1.5C threshold could be exceeded around 2030. “There are no good outcomes in exceeding 1.5C,” said glaciologist James Kirkham, lead author of one of the reports, entitled “Overshoot and the Cryosphere”, which was written with 80 scientists. “To contain the global fallout and damage from ice loss in the world’s polar and mountain regions, overshoot needs to be kept to the absolute minimum,” he said. “Every extra fraction of a degree and every year spent in overshoot means more devastating impacts.” Urgency Scientists warn in particular about the risks of crossing certain tipping points and say that, even if temperatures were to return to below the 1.5C threshold, recovery would be very slow. Reducing warming to under 1.5C and even 1C could see some glaciers partially regenerate, while there could also be benefits for sea ice. But Matthew England, an oceanographer and climatologist at the University of New South Wales in Australia, said recovery could take “decades to centuries”. The second report — “State of the Cryosphere 2026. The Cost of Overshoot” — shows that exceeding 2.8C into the next century would have significant consequences. Sea levels could rise by up to five centimetres a year by 2150, compared to the current 0.45 centimetres while the thawing of permafrost could release as much carbon dioxide each year as the United States, the world’s second-largest polluter. A worst-case but not-so-improbable scenario is that the world is heading towards warming of 2.6C by 2100 even if countries meet their climate commitments. “Temporarily exceeding 1.5C does not mean that the goals of the Paris Agreement are irrelevant but instead makes them more urgent,” argued Kirkham. “Returning to 1.5C or below by 2100 remains possible with sufficient political ambition and urgency, specifically by speeding the transition away from fossil fuel use to reach net zero by mid-century,” he said. Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

items.title: The Multimedia Group tops 30th GJA Media Awards with nine nominations
items.description: The Multimedia Group has topped nominations for the 30th Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Media Awards, securing nine nominations across its subsidiaries ahead of the awards ceremony on Saturday, November 7, 2026. The nominations, announced on Monday, November 2, at the Ghana International Press Centre in Accra, recognise outstanding journalistic works produced in 2025. The media conglomerate has nominated seven journalists and two flagship programmes for honours in various categories. The nominees are: Clinton Yeboah – JoyNews Nathaniel Attoh – Joy Sports Emmanuel Dzivenu – JoyNews Emmanuel Bright Quaicoe – JoyNews Philip Osei Bonsu – Asempa FM Nana Boakye Yiadom – JoyNews Jemima Andoh – JoyNews Badwam – Adom TV’s morning show Ekosiisen – Asempa FM’s afternoon political and current affairs talk show The nine nominations place The Multimedia Group at the top of the nominations list for this year’s awards. The awards ceremony will take place at The Grand Arena of the Accra International Conference Centre. President John Dramani Mahama is expected to grace the occasion as Special Guest of Honour, alongside the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the GJA’s Patron. The Ga Mantse, King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, will chair the ceremony. This year’s awards will be held under the theme, “Celebrating Excellence, Advancing Media Freedom and Combating Hate Speech in the Digital Age.” According to the GJA, 327 entries were received from 206 journalists, with the nine-member Awards Committee, chaired by former Daily Graphic Editor Kobby Asmah, reviewing 326 entries across the various categories. GJA President Albert Kwabena Dwumfour says the 30th anniversary edition will celebrate journalists and media organisations whose work has contributed to Ghana’s democratic governance, national development and public accountability. The ceremony will recognise outstanding journalism across television, radio, print, online and digital media, with the prestigious P.A.V. Ansah Journalist of the Year Award among the major honours to be presented.

items.title: TRAFFITEC-GH: The good, the bad and what could be
items.description: Ghana’s roads need discipline, our drivers need guidance, and our road safety institutions need the courage to enforce the law fairly. Against this background, TRAFFITEC-GH, the proposed technology-driven traffic enforcement initiative, presents an opportunity to improve road safety, strengthen accountability and modernise how traffic offences are detected and addressed. But there is a fundamental truth about public policy: a good idea is only as good as the system that delivers it. Technology can help enforce the law, but it cannot compensate for poor road markings, missing speed-limit signs, dysfunctional traffic lights or inadequate public education. Neither can it replace fairness, transparency and common sense. As Ghana prepares to embrace a more technology-driven approach to traffic enforcement, we must welcome the promise while asking the difficult questions. The objective should not simply be to catch more motorists. It should be to make our roads safer, our institutions more credible and our citizens better informed. The Good: A necessary step towards modern enforcement The attraction of automated traffic enforcement is obvious. Properly designed systems can detect speeding, red-light violations and other specified offences with greater consistency than manual enforcement alone. They can reduce opportunities for roadside bribery, create digital evidence and help authorities identify dangerous driving patterns. There is also a potential economic benefit. Road crashes impose enormous costs on families, businesses, emergency services and the national economy. If technology helps prevent collisions, saves lives and reduces avoidable congestion, its value will extend far beyond the revenue collected from penalties. More importantly, automated enforcement can establish a culture in which drivers understand that compliance is expected everywhere, not merely where a police officer happens to be standing. However, TRAFFITEC-GH must be judged by measurable improvements in road safety, not by the number of tickets issued or the amount of money collected. A successful system should ultimately produce safer driving, fewer crashes and greater public confidence. That is the real prize. The Bad: Enforcement cannot run ahead of road readiness Here is where the conversation becomes less comfortable. A camera can detect that a vehicle is travelling at 80 kilometresper hour. But is that stretch of road properly signposted? Is the speed limit clearly visible? Has the road been designed to support that limit safely? Are temporary restrictions, roadworks and diversions properly indicated? These are not excuses for reckless driving. They are questions of fairness and sound administration. A motorist should not be expected to guess a speed limit, just as a football referee cannot reasonably punish a player for breaking a rule that was never properly communicated. The law remains the law, but effective enforcement requires clarity. The same concern applies to traffic lights. Where signals are defective, poorly maintained or completely non-functional, automated enforcement at affected junctions risks creating confusion and disputes. Drivers may be confronted with conflicting instructions from road markings, officers, damaged signals and the movement of other vehicles. And what happens at night when streetlights are not working? Visibility deteriorates, road markings become harder to see, pedestrians are less visible, and poorly illuminated signs become almost decorative. If enforcement equipment continues operating in such conditions, authorities must be able to demonstrate that the evidence is reliable and that the applicable rules were clear. The solution is not to suspend traffic laws whenever infrastructure fails. Rather, authorities must establish procedures for identifying defective junctions, suspending or adjusting automated enforcement where necessary, and urgently repairing the infrastructure. Technology must enforce a properly functioning road system, not expose the weaknesses of a neglected one. The scam before the system Perhaps the most troubling development is that fraudsters have reportedly begun exploiting public interest in TRAFFITECH-GH even before its full rollout. The scheme is straightforward and sinister: impersonate an official institution, mimic a DVLA-related website, circulate messages claiming that motorists have committed offences, and persuade unsuspecting recipients to pay fabricated fines. The advertised commencement date creates urgency, and urgency is a scammer’s favourite business partner. The Ghana Police Service has published official guidance warning that genuine Electronic Notices of Violation should carry the sender identification GPS-MTTD. It also warns motorists against suspicious messages containing clickable links and directs them to the government’s official payment platform. This warning deserves nationwide publicity. The police, the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), the National Road Safety Authority and the Cyber Security Authority should coordinate an aggressive public alert campaign. Fraudulent domains must be identified, reported and taken down promptly, while investigations should pursue those responsible. The public must also be told, repeatedly, that a convincing logo does not make a website genuine, a vehicle registration number does not prove a ticket is authentic, and an alarming SMS is not a court judgment. Motorists should never pay a traffic fine through a personal Mobile Money number or an unfamiliar payment link. They should verify suspicious notices through official channels and report suspected fraud to the police. If criminals can impersonate the enforcement system before it is fully operational, public education must address not only traffic offences but also digital fraud. Otherwise, an initiative designed to promote road discipline could inadvertently create a new market for organised deception. Education before punishment, not instead of it The decision to postpone the initial October 1 rollout to November 1, 2026, to allow additional public education was sensible. It recognises an important principle: citizens must understand a system before they can reasonably be expected to navigate its procedures confidently. But education must go beyond press conferences, radio interviews and official statements. The Police Service should partner with driving schools, transport unions, commercial drivers, motorbike riders, schools, churches, traditional authorities and the media to explain the offences, applicable penalties, notification procedures and appeal mechanisms. Information should be available in accessible language, including Ghanaian languages, and should reach drivers who do not regularly use smartphones or the internet. Motorists must also understand that receiving a notice does not remove their right to challenge an alleged offence. The process should be straightforward, affordable and transparent. The remaining days before November 1 should therefore be used intensively. If operational readiness, public understanding or infrastructure conditions prove inadequate at particular locations, authorities should consider a phased approach rather than allowing a national deadline to override practical realities. A stronger implementation in 2027 may be achievable if the closing months of 2026 are used to identify weaknesses, repair infrastructure, test procedures and build public confidence. That is not an argument for abandoning enforcement. It is an argument for getting it right. What must change for TRAFFITECH-GH to work Five practical measures deserve immediate attention. 1. Audit the roads. Inspect every enforcement corridor and relevant junction for functioning traffic lights, visible speed-limit signs, clear road markings, adequate lighting and properly maintained road signs. Publish a schedule for correcting defects. 2. Guarantee accuracy. Maintain human verification of captured evidence, reliable equipment calibration, secure records and independent audits. Every notice should identify the alleged offence, time, location (Not just GPS co-ordinates), vehicle and applicable penalty. 3. Protect motorists’ rights. Provide accessible channels to view evidence, challenge errors, correct vehicle ownership records and obtain timely decisions. False penalties must be withdrawnpromptly. 4. Fight fraud aggressively. Publish verified official channels, work with telecommunications companies to flag impersonation attempts, and prosecute offenders. Public warnings should be repeated throughout the rollout. 5. Measure the right outcomes. Report on crashes, injuries, compliance, system errors, successful appeals and infrastructure repairs. Transparency will help the public distinguish a safety programme from a revenue-collection exercise. These measures require coordination among the Police Service, DVLA, the National Road Safety Authority, road authorities, local assemblies and the relevant cybersecurity institutions. The Verdict: Good Idea, Better Execution TRAFFITEC-GH has the potential to improve road safety, but its success depends on effective execution, public education, sound infrastructure and institutional accountability. Political loyalty should never replace objective scrutiny, just as opposition should not dismiss a potentially beneficial initiative. Enforcement must be firm but fair, transparent and accessible. Ultimately, success should be measured not by fines issued, but by lives saved and accidents prevented. The cameras may watch the roads, but creating safer roads remains a shared responsibility.

items.title: Imported wheat fails to cut flour prices
items.description: KARACHI: Although the arrival of imported wheat has brought down prices in the open market, consumers continue to pay high prices for different varieties of flour and Roti. On Oct 28, when the first ship carrying 51,000 tonnes of wheat berthed at the port, wheat prices in the open market plunged to Rs130 from Rs140 per kilogram. Another ship carrying 58,132 tonnes is due at Karachi today (Tuesday). Wheat prices in the open market started fluctuating in the open market after arrival of the imported grain. Market stakeholders quoted different rates. According to wholesalers, the average price stood at Rs132 per kg, while millers say that rates hovered between Rs136 and Rs137 per kg. Millers had raised the prices of different varieties of flour by Rs20 per kg, but later brought down prices ahead of the arrival of imported wheat. A miller claimed that all the mills had reduced prices on Oct 28, two days ahead of the ship’s arrival. The latest mill prices of flour No 2.5, Maida and fine flour are Rs156, Rs168 and Rs171, respectively, while the rates during the first week of October were Rs161, Rs173 and Rs176, respectively. No relief for consumer But consumers have yet to get any relief as the rates for Chapati, Naan, Sheermal/Taftaan and Qulcha remain unchanged at Rs20, Rs30-35, Rs100-110 and Rs90-100, respectively. A tandoor owner said the high price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) (Rs500-550 per kg) has offset the impact of reduction in flour prices. “It will be hard to sustain our operations in case LPG prices go up further,” he said. Likewise, the retail rates for flour No 2.5 and Maida remained unchanged at Rs170-180 and Rs185-190, while fine flour sold Rs185-190 per kg. Rauf Ibrahim, a wholesaler, said the regulator has been unable to check inflated retail rates despite a dip in the open market. He said the import of 750,000 tonnes of wheat will turn out to be insufficient as the country needs over two million tonnes to bridge the demand and supply gap as the new crops from Sindh and Punjab will arrive only between March and May. Ibrahim urged the government to allow the private sector and flour millers to import grain in order to stabilise flour prices. He said the lives of workers earning below Rs50,000 have become miserable since they have to spend almost the entire income on putting food on the table, leaving little for their children’s education and other needs. Disparity in prices Consumers living in Karachi and Hyderabad are paying the highest prices for flour varieties compared to other cities across the country. As per the Sensitive Price Index (SPI) ending Oct 29, a 20kg flour bag in Karachi costs up to Rs3,540 while its average price in other parts of the country is Rs3,200. Hyderabad holds the second spot where the price of a 20kg bag ranges between Rs3,360 and Rs3,400. In Islamabad, Rawa­lpindi, Lahore and other major Punjab cities, prices ranged between Rs2,200 and Rs3,333. Wheat rates Sukkur is much ahead in terms of wheat rates as a 10kg bag sells for Rs1,488, while Peshawar holds the second spot with a rate of Rs1,469. The third highest rate of Rs1,453 prevails in Hyderabad. In Karachi the 10kg bag is available at Rs1,440. In Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the average price is Rs1,453. The lowest rate for a 10kg bag is in Sargodha with Rs1,223, followed by Bahawalpur with Rs1,266 and Rs1,300 in Faisalabad and Sialkot. Fine Atta Consumers in Hyderabad and Quetta are paying the highest rate of Rs187 per kg, followed by Rs185 per kg being paid by the people of Karachi. The third highest rate of Rs183 per kg prevails in Islamabad. In other cities, the average price of one kilogram of fine flour ranged between Rs147 and Rs180 per kg. A flour miller said that one of the reasons for high prices in Karachi is that the city is not a wheat-growing area and is dependent on the arrival of grain from the rest of Sindh. Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

items.title: Traffitech: Katanomics can turn smart ideas into absurdities
items.description: Traffitech-GH went live on 1 November . Almost immediately, five Ghanaian transport unions declared a strike for 4 November . Despite framing their grievances around poor road traffic infrastructure, a pointed line in their statement makes it clear what the fight is really about: “We cannot operate in bus stops occupied by traders and still be fined by cameras.” When the idea of automating fines for bad driving using cameras first reared its head, I asked if the Police can truly transcend katanomics . I asked because katanomics can turn even brilliant, obvious, and inevitable ideas into a mess of absurdities. If the road network and ancillary structures themselves are disorganised, it becomes unreasonable to automate fines as if each offence is straightforward. A major part of why current manual police enforcement of traffic rules is the way it is is that it has to apply judgement to adjust strict rules to the reality of a pervasive physical mess. But the state has chosen to bring a very modern way to punish people for disorder caused by a very old mess. Standard katanomics. The “WHAT” is always easy to sell. In this case, it is simply “stop the carnage”. And the carnage is real. Road crashes killed 2,949 people in 2025 , the highest in 35 years. Who can oppose “doing something about it”? But as katanomics teaches, we always pay little attention to “the HOW”. So it escapes scrutiny, and every awkward question gets treated as an attack on progress. This mindset of thinking that intentions and attempts are enough is the biggest impediment to real progress in Ghana because those who call it out would always come across as unreasonable. Other times, sloppy preparatory work is excused with the argument that it is best to start and improve later. Which isn’t totally ridiculous except that it presumes that national learning is a giving. The whole mission of katanomics is to show how and why such learning almost never happens. Citizens should just look around them and pay attention to the whole host of initiatives that were began on just this premise and stayed sloppy forever. Remember a certain sugar factory ? Now that the cameras are rolling, the awkward questions about Traffitech will continue to multiply. I am writing this piece purely for future reference. And as part of the documentation for teaching katanomics. Guess the limit The MTTD now concedes that Traffitech-GH is limited to speeding and that “[for] other offences, we will continue to enforce them manually” . In August, the Interior Minister was telling us it covered more than 47 offences . Essentially, all the rancour is about addressing, what, 2% of the problem? Hard to say, as research into which offences cause the most harm hasn’t been conducted for eons. But even with respect to speeding, the most basic question confronting every driver as the system rolls out has been left murky: how fast am I allowed to go here? The Police FAQ gives four answers: 50 km/h in built-up areas, 90 on highways, 100 on motorways, and 30 km/h within a school, playground, health facility, church, mosque, market, shopping centre or procession, or “anywhere human activity is predominant”. Try to picture Accra or Kumasi as you read those words. How exactly does a zone of predominant human activity look like? Where does one begin and end? Does a highway become a market zone when the hawkers surge in? At what point does the driver accelerate again? In classic katanomic and state enchantment fashion, the state has bought cameras to measure speed to the kilometre but left motorists to figure out on their own the geography of offending. The FAQ does promise signs at the start of enforced corridors and at “selected points” along them. Then it strips the promise of any value: “A licensed driver must be conversant with the above whether or not a speed-limit sign is posted.” And, of course, at launch time, the signs were nowhere to be found. When drivers complain about faulty street & traffic lights and missing signs, ACP Alexander Obeng of the Police MTTD replies: “We should not mix the issues up.” Seriously? On day one, ACP Obeng gave the game away. Announcing that some drivers had done over 130 km/h on Mahama Road, a 50 km/h road, he warned: “when the road is straight and flat in the city, don’t think it is a highway.” That is a policeman conceding that the road itself tells drivers one thing while the law says another. The usual remedy for that is called a sign. It gets murkier because the police intend to rely heavily on moving cameras. The launch briefing confirmed that cameras have been placed in unmarked police vehicles and on tripods . But there is a world of difference between concealing the policeman and concealing the rule. CUTS International pointed out that L.I. 2519 itself provides for signage alongside speed cameras and asked that limits be posted before every camera. Clearly, as will soon become clear, the ambiguity is deliberately designed to serve the project’s financial goals. The argument that motorists ought to know the rules by heart is rather rich. The revised Highway Code , launched in October 2023 to replace a version from 1974, predates the 2026 regulations and it shows. It has no provisions to cater for such dynamic shifts. I doubt many have considered the issue of the speed units either. About 90 per cent of cars on Ghana’s roads are imported used vehicles , and many come from the United States, where speedometers tend to be set to miles per hour. The few signs that do exist only display a bare number, without units. As one safety professional noted in the Chronicle , a driver who sees “50” and holds steady at 50 on an American dial is actually driving at about 80 km/h. None of this was unforeseen. In April 2018, the President’s road-safety plan promised GH¢335 million a year, for three years, for signs and road markings . Eight years later, the state has pushed out the fines. The signs may come later. Even the price is a guess You would think the fine, at least, would be clear. The graduated schedule for automated offences under Regulation 242 starts at GH¢120 for each of the first three offences . But in October, ACP Obeng told listeners that for speeding, “any 5 kilometers per hour above the limit… the penalty starts at 20 penalty units” , that is GH¢240, and rising. Other explainers put speeding at GH¢240 to GH¢480 . Clearly, the murkiness is structural. At least, the formula for late payments is more straightforward. If also brutal. After 14 days, 1 per cent of the fine is added for every day of default , with no published ceiling. That is a simple annual rate of ~365 per cent. A GH¢240 fine thus becomes GH¢480 after 100 days of default and GH¢1,116 after a year. Meanwhile, amidst all this, the Roads Minister told Parliament in June that the state owes the companies that maintain traffic signals about GH¢40 million . The government doesn’t mind piling up arrears on the traffic lights needed for road safety, but drivers better not even dream of owing. Looking in the wrong place The next absurdity is geographic. Ghana’s road deaths are not, mostly, a downtown Accra problem. In 2025, Ashanti recorded 692 deaths and Eastern 649, against 420 for Greater Accra , even though Greater Accra had the most crashes. The difference is lethality. The Eastern Region recorded 28 deaths per 100 crashes; Greater Accra recorded 10. People die on the long intercity stretches, at highway speeds, in head-on collisions and in the dark. Even inside the capital, the city’s Accra Road Safety Report 2024 is clear on where to focus. Of 118 deaths in the Accra Metropolitan Area that year, 76 per cent happened on highways within the city, such as the N1, not on ordinary town streets. Hotspots included the Kwashieman intersection and the Ring Road Central corridor. More deaths occurred between 8 and 10 at night than in any other two-hour window, and half came on weekends. Vulnerable road users (pedestrians, motorcyclists and cyclists) were 86 per cent of the dead. No one is saying that speeding in Accra isn’t an issue. Observational studies found that, on monitored roads in 2024, between 44 and 49 per cent of vehicles were over the limit . The question is whether a few dozen mobile camera units, launched first in towns, are aimed at tackling the deaths based on evidence or at opportunities to fine lots of people quickly. We asked the Police to publish the deployment plan against the crash map, including evening and weekend coverage, so the public can tell a safety hotspot from a profitable camera position. Didn’t happen. We should also not lose sight of pedestrians in these conversations. They account for about a third of all road deaths nationally . Currently, Traffitech can’t fine a pedestrian. Nor does a photograph of a collision course change the collision course. What is sorely needed are usable pavements, refuge islands, and raised crossing. Few would disagree that motorcycles are the biggest blind spot. The NRSA says 226 of Greater Accra’s 420 road deaths in 2025 , 54 per cent, involved motorbikes. In a single July operation against racing on the George Walker Bush Highway near Villaggio, police impounded 71 motorcycles, 26 of them unregistered . The DVLA says about 5 per cent of all number plates in use are fake , often copied from wrecked cars. How will Traffitech text registered owners when registration records don’t exist? The properly documented motorist thus becomes conveniently billable. While undocumented menaces continue to roam the street, unpoliced. Meanwhile, many of the deadliest highway behaviours in Accra are not even very susceptible to automated camera enforcement. A speed gun cannot judge an overtake on a blind bend, fatigue at the wheel, or why someone swerved. All this takes evidence and judgement, and you can’t delegate it to a single speed reading. The lights are out Apparently red-light cameras will come later. But some of the issues are comical. An April 2026 Department of Urban Roads assessment found only 257 of 411 traffic signal installations working . A 2025 survey by the National Safety Campaign found only 13 per cent of traffic lights in Accra and surrounding cities fully functional . The Roads Minister blames people stripping signal parts for scrap , while the maintenance firms wait for their GH¢40 million. CUTS found signals near the Apenkwa overpass and the Police Training Academy junction in Tesano shifted out of clear view while the cameras appeared correctly positioned . Total confusion. The Accra Intelligent Traffic Management System was part of a US$210.6 million China Development Bank loan that Ghana has collected and, as we say in these parts, chopped . In 2020, its US$100 million traffic contract was handed to Huawei under the Ministry of National Security . Its second phase is 23 per cent complete, held up by legal disputes, with a US$55 million judgement debt attached . Finding money to keep the rules working is apparently a headache. So, why not just find investors to charge people for flouting those same rules? Do you know your ringtone? Traffitech fines are issued in an SMS to the registered car owner. That, naturally, assumes a well-functioning registry with an up-to-date owner phone directory. Yet, the government’s 2024 PPP report on the Traffitech project found missing owner information in DVLA records and insurance files still stuck with brokers’ phone numbers . The Police FAQ adds that if you sold your car, you remain liable until the DVLA records the change of ownership and phone number . (By the way, the DVLA will re-register all four million-plus vehicles with new plates between January 2027 and December 2028 .) Until then, expect a lot of people to rack up fines without knowing that they are. Because the registered owner is liable “regardless of who was driving” . And a sixth offence within 24 months can cost a driving licence for at least a year. Whose licence, when several drivers share an owner’s trotro, a rental car or a company fleet? Trotro drivers typically rent the bus daily from an owner for a fixed “sales” fee and drive harder to make the target. SMS fine notices will go to owners, who will be saddled with the headaches of appeals in a chaotic system. To dispute or appeal, the owner must start online within 14 days, choose an MTTD station, wait for an appointment, and then a court hearing is scheduled . The FAQ says that while they contest a fine, owners will continue to owe the fine plus any accumulated late penalty . The police have no deadline to resolve a dispute/appeal. Faced with a small wrong fine, a rational person compares the cost of capitulation with the cost of vindication. The law-abiding will almost always capitulate. The rascals will take their chances. The deterrent against failing to pay is that the DVLA will not process licence renewal, registration, transfer, or roadworthiness inspection . Once again, something likely to pinch law-abiding citizens whilst those who bribe their way through shrug it off. But the logic itself is questionable. We want unsafe vehicles inspected. So we will refuse to inspect them until they clear their fine debt. Making the safety inspection part of the collateral in a collection dispute is a remarkable way to protect road users. The scam story is almost comic. Police arrested seven people in February for sending fake fine notices with payment links . The Police FAQ now warns that any message with a clickable link is likely a scam . Yet the launch briefing said every genuine notice comes with a link to the video evidence . How? The Money Factor Much of the confusion stems from the fact that money is a big part of the whole ensemble. Which also explains why the infrastructure is an afterthought. Traffitech-GH is a public-private partnership signed in December 2022 with Nationwide Traffic Management and Enforcement Ltd (NTMEL), 60 per cent owned by entrepreneur Frank Osei and 40 per cent by the Swedish-listed Sensys Gatso . The commercial commitment came three years before Parliament passed the December 2025 amendment that made automated fines lawful. The Ministry of Finance anticipates a revenue split of 40 per cent to the private party and 60 per cent to government , and its 2022 report lists “revenues from traffic fines for Government” among the benefits to maximise. Sensys Gatso has told its investors to expect about SEK 600 million in joint-venture revenue over the remaining term , roughly US$60 million, and says the programme now enters “a ramp-up period requiring additional investment”. Do the sums. If that is the operator’s 40 per cent, Ghanaians must pay about US$150 million in fines by 2033. At the September rate of GH¢11.55 to the dollar , that is roughly GH¢1.7 billion, or about 7 million speeding tickets at GH¢240. Basic arithmetic says we need at least 2,700 fines a day, every day, for seven years. That’s the easy part: squeezing citizens for their hard-earned cash. The problem is that this motive will often clash with common sense. Every fine prevented by a clearer sign, a working traffic light or street light, or a redesigned junction is money lost to highly motivated investors looking to cash in on a lucrative contract. Economists and others have a term for this: perverse incentives. If the scheme succeeds at safety, drivers comply, violations fall and the business model weakens, which then makes the whole project unsustainable. The operator’s interest and the public’s interest now point in opposite directions. The American federal guide on speed cameras insists that vendors should not even be involved in selecting sites, “to avoid any real or perceived influence on program revenues” . In Ghana, the vendor is the operator. The Police have already presented September’s figures (crashes down from 1,108 to 1,003, deaths from 243 to 224 against September 2025) as a pilot achievement . The problem is that we have only the Police’s word, and right now they are an interested party. Independent bodies are much too under-resourced to collect their own statistics. It is therefore not surprising that the Police’s stats do not include data on enforced sites against comparable untreated ones, false notices, and overturned tickets. An eleven-year concession needs an evaluation system that can report on failures. Perhaps wishful thinking, as independent bodies are starved of resources while interested parties collect evaluation data. In 2025, as road deaths climbed to a 35-year high, the National Road Safety Authority blamed the rise partly on its own inactivity, as it lacked the resources even to run campaigns . The state basically has no resources to fund its safety regulator. Priority sequencing Sensys Gatso likes to invoke Vision Zero , the Swedish road-safety philosophy. But how really does Sweden do it? Its transport administration runs a “no hidden cameras” policy, with road signs and speed signs before each camera site, and credits the cameras with cutting fatalities by 20 to 30 per cent at the sites. The notice goes to the driver identified from the photograph while the owner is only asked who was driving . Ghana imported the Swedish camera business with little enthusiasm for the Swedish road authority’s obligations or for Sweden’s capacity to run a sophisticated automated fining system. Uganda’s version, with a reported 80 per cent cut for its operator , was suspended within days after it became clear that the country simply wasn’t ready infrastructure-wise. But credit where credit is due: Accra has a homegrown model. At the Holy Spirit Cathedral intersection , the city repainted markings, narrowed the junction, lowered kerbs, installed speed-limit signs and fixed bollards to stop motorcycles riding through crossings. Clearly, Ghana can get things done when serious people commit. So here is a more sensible order of work. Link enforcement to impact. Put clearly signposted cameras, including average-speed systems, on the intercity corridors where most of the killings occur, and in the key urban hotspots. Publish a risk map and ensure transparent deployment so everyone can see it. This will build trust, especially with transport unions like GPRTU, whose members will bear the brunt of this system. Sign before you fine. No automated ticket on any segment without a posted speed limit, in km/h, besides the camera. Switch the lights on. Pay the maintenance firms, finish the already-financed signal system, and make every red-light camera conditional on a working, visible traffic light signal. While you’re at it, fix the streetlights too. Fix the physical mess along with the behavioural mess. Clear and protect bus stops, as the unions demand and the law requires. Copy the Holy Spirit Cathedral redesign along the deadly corridors. Make motorcycle registration, visible plates, proper helmets, and impaired-driving checks central, and create a model in which police are stationed at priority hotspots. Fix the contract. First, publish the contract for public scrutiny. Second, pay the operator an audited service fee with performance conditions, so improved compliance doesn’t undermine its income. Publish calibration certificates and clear rules to ensure no abuse of camera feed and car movement data. . Site-level outcomes must be openly published every quarter. Ensure fairness. Allow an independently adjudicated first appeal online, and freeze the penalty clock within the set determination period. A proper driver registry needs to be built to ensure notices reach the actual driver. Roadworthiness inspections should not be held hostage to fine arrears Accra’s road chaos must continue to be treated as a pure problem to be solved. No one must be allowed to turn it into a cash cow. My bet, as ever with katanomics, is that if the elite behave as they always do, it’s the cash cow. But I would very much like to lose that bet.

items.title: Housing deficit falls to 1.8 million, but service gaps remain — GSS
items.description: Ghana’s estimated housing deficit declined from 2.8 million units in 2010 to 1.8 million in 2021, but persistent gaps in access to electricity, sanitation and decent settlement conditions continue to affect households across the country. The Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) says the improvement in the housing shortfall has not eliminated the challenges associated with the availability and distribution of homes and basic services, particularly as the country’s urban population continues to grow. The figures are contained in the Ghana in Numbers, 2025 , a flagship publication released by the Service on November 2, which brings together population, housing and basic-service indicators to guide development planning. According to the report, the 2021 Population and Housing Census counted about 10 million dwelling units, while the estimated housing deficit stood at approximately 1.8 million units. The GSS, however, cautioned that the deficit was an estimate based on the number of homes required and available. It did not, on its own, measure housing quality, affordability or the number of vacant homes. Basic-service gaps persist Despite improvements in access to essential services over the years, the report identifies significant gaps in household access to electricity and improved sanitation. The proportion of households with electricity increased from 43.8 per cent in 2000 to 86.3 per cent in 2021. Access to improved drinking water also rose from 60.7 per cent to 92 per cent over the same period, while improved sanitation increased from 44.8 per cent in 2010 to 69 per cent in 2022. Nevertheless, about one in seven households still has no electricity, while almost one in three lacks an improved toilet. The report further indicates that 30.8 per cent of Ghana’s urban population lives in slums or informal settlements, underscoring the uneven conditions in which many urban residents live. Smaller households, rising housing needs The GSS also reported that the average household size had fallen to 3.6 people, the lowest recorded level. It explained that the decline in household size could increase the number of homes required, even when population growth slows, as more households would need separate accommodation. The trend has implications for housing demand and urban planning, particularly as the country’s urban population expands. About 19.8 million people, representing 58.7 per cent of Ghana’s population, lived in urban areas in 2025, according to the report. Ghana became more urban than rural in 2010, when 12.55 million people lived in urban areas, compared with 12.11 million in rural communities. By 2021, the urban population had risen to 17.47 million, against 13.36 million in rural areas. GSS urges localised planning Government Statistician, Dr Alhassan Iddrisu, said the statistics should guide decisions on the provision of housing and essential services at the community level. “Use local figures, not national averages, to decide where the next cedi goes, because averages hide differences,” he said. He said population data should help determine “where schools, clinics and homes must go”, stressing the importance of using local evidence to identify communities with the greatest needs. The Service said district-level figures could help policymakers identify areas where gaps in housing, water, sanitation, electricity and other services were most pronounced. The Ghana in Numbers, 2025 publication and related district data are available through the GSS website, StatsBank, the Ghana in Numbers web portal and the GSS Stats App.
